examples: The desks were set up in a U-shaped arrangement.
A U-shaped valley was carved out by a glacier.
The driveway is U-shaped, so you never have to back up.

entries.meaning: Found everywhere; seeming to be in every place at once. ---
examples: Cell phones are ubiquitous now.
Those ubiquitous orange cones mean road work ahead.
Coffee shops are more ubiquitous here than anywhere else I've lived.

entries.meaning: From Uganda, or having to do with Uganda. ---
examples: He teaches at a Ugandan university.
The Ugandan team won the relay.
Her parents are Ugandan.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person from Uganda: he's a Ugandan.

entries.meaning: Hidden, and different from the reason a person gives. ---
examples: I think he has an ulterior motive for helping.
She offered with no ulterior purpose at all.
There's always some ulterior reason with that family.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: an ulterior motive
entries.contrast: Almost always in ulterior motive — a hidden reason behind a friendly-looking act.

entries.meaning: Ultimate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ultimate decision is hers.
Our ultimate goal is to get everyone housed.
It's the ultimate road trip.
That's the ultimate compliment, coming from her.

senses.head: Final; coming at the end of a process
examples: The ultimate decision is hers.
Our ultimate goal is to get everyone housed.

senses.head: The best or greatest of its kind
examples: It's the ultimate road trip.
That's the ultimate compliment, coming from her.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the ultimate goal
entries.contrast: Also a noun in the ultimate in + noun: the ultimate in comfort.

entries.meaning: Far to the right politically, or strongly opposed to any change. ---
examples: He writes for an ultraconservative magazine.
Her views on schooling are ultraconservative.
The district keeps electing ultraconservative candidates.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person: the ultraconservatives in the party.

entries.meaning: Of light waves just beyond violet, which the eye cannot see but which burn skin. ---
examples: Sunscreen blocks ultraviolet rays.
They check the bills under an ultraviolet lamp.
Ultraviolet light kills bacteria on the surface.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: ultraviolet light
entries.contrast: Shortened to UV in everyday talk: UV rays, UV index.

entries.meaning: A large but uncounted number of. ---
examples: I've told you umpteen times to close the door.
There are umpteen ways to do this.
She has umpteen cousins in Ohio.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: umpteen times
entries.contrast: Informal, and always a vague 'a lot' — you never say how many, and you cannot count them.

entries.meaning: Coming after a large, uncounted number of others. ---
examples: For the umpteenth time, no.
This is the umpteenth meeting about the same thing.
He was watching the umpteenth rerun of that show.
entries.position: attributive only — after the: the umpteenth time
entries.contrast: Nearly always in for the umpteenth time, said in exasperation.

entries.meaning: Against what the speaker takes to be American values. ---
examples: He called the protest un-American.
Censorship is un-American, they argued.
Nothing is more un-American than telling people how to pray.
entries.contrast: A political insult, not a neutral word: it means 'against American values', not 'not from America'.

entries.meaning: Not at all embarrassed or ashamed, where most people would be. ---
examples: She's an unabashed fan of bad movies.
He was completely unabashed about asking for more money.
There was unabashed joy on their faces.

entries.meaning: Going on at full strength, without getting any weaker. ---
examples: The rain continued unabated all night.
Demand for tickets was unabated.
Unabated construction has changed the whole neighborhood.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: the rain continued unabated

entries.meaning: Printed or recorded complete, with nothing cut out. ---
examples: I listened to the unabridged audiobook.
It's the unabridged edition, all nine hundred pages.
The text on this page is unabridged.

entries.meaning: So bad or wrong that you cannot allow it. ---
examples: That kind of language is unacceptable here.
The delay is unacceptable to our customers.
They sent back an unacceptable offer.

entries.meaning: Unaccompanied has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Unaccompanied minors have to check in at the desk.
Children under twelve may not ride unaccompanied.
She sang the last verse unaccompanied.
It's a piece for unaccompanied cello.

senses.head: With nobody going along
examples: Unaccompanied minors have to check in at the desk.
Children under twelve may not ride unaccompanied.

senses.head: Of music: sung or played with no instruments behind it
examples: She sang the last verse unaccompanied.
It's a piece for unaccompanied cello.

entries.meaning: Unaccountable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: For some unaccountable reason, he turned around and left.
There was an unaccountable delay at the border.
The agency is unaccountable to voters.
Power that is unaccountable gets abused.

senses.head: Impossible to explain
examples: For some unaccountable reason, he turned around and left.
There was an unaccountable delay at the border.

senses.head: Not having to answer to anyone for what you do
examples: The agency is unaccountable to voters.
Power that is unaccountable gets abused.

entries.takes: to + noun, in the second sense

entries.meaning: Unaccustomed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was unaccustomed to the heat.
She's unaccustomed to being told no.
He spoke with unaccustomed warmth.
There was an unaccustomed quiet in the house.

senses.head: Not used to something
examples: He was unaccustomed to the heat.
She's unaccustomed to being told no.

senses.head: Not usual; not what that person normally does
examples: He spoke with unaccustomed warmth.
There was an unaccustomed quiet in the house.

entries.meaning: Impossible to reach or carry out. ---
examples: The deadline was unachievable from the start.
They set an unachievable target and then blamed the staff.
Nothing here is unachievable if we start now.

entries.meaning: Not admitted, not noticed, or not thanked for. ---
examples: Her work went unacknowledged for years.
There's an unacknowledged rule about where people sit.
My email is still unacknowledged.

entries.meaning: Of a problem or a question: not dealt with. ---
examples: The safety issues went unaddressed for months.
Several unaddressed complaints are still in the file.
That part of the question is unaddressed in the report.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: the problem went unaddressed

entries.meaning: Plain, with nothing added for decoration. ---
examples: The room was white and unadorned.
He gave the unadorned facts and sat down.
It's a simple, unadorned wooden box.

entries.meaning: Unadulterated has 2 distinct senses.

They sell unadulterated honey straight from the hive.
The oil is unadulterated — nothing in it but olives.

examples: That is pure, unadulterated nonsense.
The look on his face was unadulterated joy.

senses.head: Of food or drink: pure, with nothing added to it
examples: They sell unadulterated honey straight from the hive.
The oil is unadulterated — nothing in it but olives.

entries.form: un- + adulterated, from adulterate 'mix in something cheaper'

entries.meaning: Not willing to try new or risky things, and dull as a result. ---
examples: I'm pretty unadventurous when it comes to food.

The menu is more unadventurous than I expected.
entries.русский: не склонный к риску; пресный, скучный

entries.meaning: Unaffected has 2 distinct senses.

She has an unaffected way of talking to everyone.
His manner is warm and unaffected.

senses.head: Not changed or harmed by something
examples: Most of the town was unaffected by the flood.
Prices for unaffected products stayed the same.

senses.head: Natural and sincere, with no show about it
examples: She has an unaffected way of talking to everyone.
His manner is warm and unaffected.

entries.contrast: In the second sense the opposite is affected 'putting on an act', not 'influenced'.

entries.meaning: Not belonging to or connected with a particular organization or party. ---

Unaffiliated voters can't vote in the primary.
He's registered as unaffiliated.

entries.meaning: Not frightened. ---
examples: She walked right up to the dog, completely unafraid.
He was unafraid of losing the job.
They're unafraid to say what they think.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: she seemed unafraid

entries.meaning: Without help from anyone or anything. ---
examples: A week later she was walking unaided.
The comet is visible to the unaided eye.
He finished the puzzle unaided.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: he walked unaided
entries.contrast: Also fixed in the unaided eye — without a telescope, microscope or glasses.

entries.meaning: Of a right: that cannot be taken away or given up. ---
examples: The Declaration speaks of certain unalienable rights.
They call free speech an unalienable right.
Those are unalienable liberties, the judge wrote.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: unalienable rights
entries.contrast: Inalienable is the ordinary modern word; unalienable survives mainly because the Declaration of Independence used it.

entries.meaning: Exactly as it was before; not changed. ---
examples: The recipe has come down unaltered for a hundred years.
His opinion remains unaltered.
They published the unaltered transcript.

entries.meaning: Having only one possible meaning; perfectly clear. ---

The evidence is clear and unambiguous.

entries.meaning: Agreed on by everyone, with nobody against it. ---
examples: The vote was unanimous.
The jury reached a unanimous verdict.
The committee was unanimous in recommending her.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the word starts yoo-, not oo-.

entries.meaning: Happening with no warning that it was coming. ---
examples: He showed up at the door unannounced.
There was an unannounced inspection on Tuesday.
She left unannounced sometime in the night.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: he showed up unannounced

senses.head: That cannot be answered
examples: Kids ask unanswerable questions.
Why some people recover and others don't is unanswerable right now.

senses.head: That cannot be argued against
examples: The case against him is unanswerable.
She made an unanswerable argument for waiting.

entries.meaning: That nobody has replied to or explained. ---
examples: My letter went unanswered.
There are still a lot of unanswered questions.

entries.position: both — often after a verb: the letter went unanswered

entries.meaning: Not expected, and so not planned for. ---
examples: The trip had a few unanticipated expenses.
An unanticipated snowstorm closed the airport.
The side effects were entirely unanticipated.

entries.meaning: Not sorry, and not pretending to be. ---
examples: He's completely unapologetic about the way he votes.
She wrote an unapologetic defense of the program.
The music is loud and unapologetic.

entries.meaning: Not attractive or pleasant; not something anyone would want. ---
examples: Both options are unappealing.
Cold eggs make an unappealing breakfast.
The idea of another meeting is deeply unappealing.

entries.meaning: Looking or smelling as though it would not taste good. ---
examples: The soup looked gray and unappetizing.
It was an unappetizing pile of something on the plate.
Cafeteria food is famously unappetizing.
entries.contrast: American spelling is -izing; British books write unappetising.

entries.meaning: Not thanked for or valued as much as deserved. ---
examples: She quit because she felt unappreciated.
His years of work went largely unappreciated.
It's an unappreciated little museum on a side street.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: she felt unappreciated

entries.meaning: Seeming cold or distant, so that people are afraid to start a conversation. ---
examples: The new manager comes across as unapproachable.

She's friendlier than she looks — not unapproachable at all.

entries.meaning: Feeling no shame about something other people might think you should. ---
examples: He's unashamed of where he came from.
It was an unashamed attempt to get attention.
She's unashamed about loving bad TV.

entries.meaning: So strong that it cannot be attacked or argued against. ---
examples: By halftime they had an unassailable lead.
Her reputation was unassailable.
The logic of the argument is unassailable.

entries.meaning: Modest and quiet; not trying to seem important. ---
examples: He's a quiet, unassuming man who happens to run the company.
The restaurant is small and unassuming.
She was the most unassuming person in the room.
entries.contrast: Praise, not criticism: it means modest, not weak.

entries.meaning: Unattached has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Most of her friends are still unattached.
He came to the wedding unattached.
One wire was left unattached.
The garage is unattached to the house.

senses.head: Not married and not in a relationship
examples: Most of her friends are still unattached.
He came to the wedding unattached.

senses.head: Not joined or connected to anything
examples: One wire was left unattached.
The garage is unattached to the house.

entries.русский: свободный, не состоящий в отношениях; неприкреплённый
entries.takes: to + noun, in the second sense

For most families that price is simply unattainable.
He set himself an unattainable goal and then gave up.

entries.meaning: Left with nobody watching or looking after it. ---
examples: Do not leave your bags unattended.
An unattended campfire started the whole thing.
The register was unattended for ten minutes.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: don't leave bags unattended

entries.meaning: Unattractive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's not unattractive, just not my type.

Both options look unattractive from here.

senses.head: Not good-looking
examples: He's not unattractive, just not my type.
It's an unattractive building on a beautiful street.

senses.head: Not appealing as a choice or an offer
examples: The terms of the loan are unattractive.
Both options look unattractive from here.

entries.meaning: Done or made without official permission. ---

Someone made an unauthorized charge on my card.
The biography is unauthorized.
entries.contrast: American spelling is -ized; British books write unauthorised.

entries.meaning: Unavailable has 2 distinct senses.

He's unavailable until Thursday.

senses.head: Not able to be had, bought or seen
examples: That size is unavailable right now.
The records are unavailable to the public.

senses.head: Of a person: not free to talk to or meet
examples: She was unavailable for comment.
He's unavailable until Thursday.

entries.meaning: Impossible to prevent or get out of. ---
examples: A short delay is unavoidable.

entries.meaning: Unbalanced has 2 distinct senses.

An unbalanced diet will catch up with you.
The letters came from someone clearly unbalanced.
His lawyer argued that he was mentally unbalanced.

senses.head: Not giving equal weight to each side; uneven
examples: The coverage was unbalanced — one side got all the airtime.
An unbalanced diet will catch up with you.

senses.head: Mentally disturbed
examples: The letters came from someone clearly unbalanced.
His lawyer argued that he was mentally unbalanced.

entries.contrast: The 'mentally ill' sense is old-fashioned and unkind; careful writers avoid it.

entries.meaning: Too painful, unpleasant or annoying to put up with. ---
examples: The heat was unbearable by noon.
He's unbearable when he loses.
The waiting was the most unbearable part.

entries.meaning: Unbeatable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: At home, that team is unbeatable.
She had an unbeatable record that season.
They advertise unbeatable prices on tires.
The location is unbeatable.

senses.head: Impossible to defeat
examples: At home, that team is unbeatable.
She had an unbeatable record that season.

senses.head: Better than anything else — of a price, an offer or a spot
examples: They advertise unbeatable prices on tires.
The location is unbeatable.

entries.meaning: Having lost no games or races so far. ---
examples: They're unbeaten going into the playoffs.
It's the school's first unbeaten season in thirty years.
His record in that weight class is still unbeaten.
entries.contrast: Unbeaten is a fact — nobody has beaten them yet; unbeatable is a judgment — nobody can.

entries.meaning: Not suitable for a person in that position; slightly shameful. ---
examples: That kind of sniping is unbecoming in a senator.
He was fired for conduct unbecoming a teacher.
There was an unbecoming eagerness in the way he agreed.
entries.contrast: In the military phrase conduct unbecoming an officer it follows the noun and takes no preposition. The older sense 'not flattering' (an unbecoming hat) now sounds dated.

entries.meaning: Without a particular person knowing about it. ---
examples: Unbeknownst to his parents, he'd dropped two classes.
The meeting had been moved, unbeknownst to half the staff.
She had been paying the bill for years, unbeknownst to him.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always in the fixed phrase unbeknownst to + person
entries.form: un- + beknownst, an old form of known
entries.contrast: Only ever used in unbeknownst to someone — you cannot say an unbeknownst fact.

entries.meaning: Unbelievable has 2 distinct senses.

His excuse was frankly unbelievable.
The whole story is unbelievable.

senses.head: So surprising, good or bad that it is hard to take in
examples: The view from up there is unbelievable.
It's unbelievable how fast kids grow.
That was the most unbelievable finish I've ever seen.

senses.head: Too unlikely to be true
examples: His excuse was frankly unbelievable.
The whole story is unbelievable.

entries.meaning: Fair, with no preference for one side over another. ---
examples: We need an unbiased account of what happened.
No news source is completely unbiased.
The new study is more unbiased than the first one.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one s: unbiased, not unbiassed.

entries.meaning: With no mark, fault or stain on it. ---
examples: He retired with an unblemished record.

examples: The cat watched him with an unblinking stare.
Her eyes were wide and unblinking.

senses.head: Looking straight at something hard or ugly without flinching
examples: It's an unblinking look at life in the camps.
He gave an unblinking account of his own mistakes.

entries.meaning: Not yet born; still inside the mother. ---
examples: She worried about her unborn baby.
The drug can harm an unborn child.
They argue about the rights of unborn children.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: her unborn child

entries.meaning: Unbreakable has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Impossible to break
examples: These plates are unbreakable, which is why we take them camping.
The new phone screen is nearly unbreakable.
Kids' cups come in unbreakable plastic.

senses.head: Impossible to end, break or beat
examples: The two sisters have an unbreakable bond.
For thirty years his home run record looked unbreakable.
She made an unbreakable promise to her mother.

entries.meaning: Not held back or controlled at all. ---
examples: The crowd greeted the team with unbridled joy.
Unbridled spending got the city into trouble.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: unbridled joy

entries.meaning: Unbroken has 2 distinct senses.

The seal on the box was still unbroken.
Only one window was unbroken after the storm.

senses.head: Going on without a stop or a gap
examples: We drove through miles of unbroken desert.
The team has an unbroken streak of eleven wins.
There was an unbroken silence in the room.

senses.head: Not broken or damaged
examples: The seal on the box was still unbroken.
Only one window was unbroken after the storm.

entries.meaning: With the buttons undone. ---
examples: His collar was unbuttoned and his tie was gone.
She came in wearing an unbuttoned coat.
He sat on the porch with his shirt unbuttoned.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: his collar was unbuttoned

entries.meaning: Rude or unfair, and not deserved by anything the other person did. ---
examples: That remark was completely uncalled-for.

He apologized for his uncalled-for comments.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: that was uncalled-for; also before a noun: an uncalled-for remark
entries.contrast: After a verb many Americans write it as two words, uncalled for; the hyphen is normal before a noun.

entries.meaning: Uncanny has 2 distinct senses.

She has an uncanny ability to guess what people are thinking.
The resemblance between the twins is uncanny.
His feel for the market is even more uncanny than his boss's.

senses.head: Strange in a way that is hard to explain and a little unsettling
examples: There was an uncanny stillness before the storm.
I had the uncanny feeling that we had met before.

senses.head: So accurate or so close that it seems impossible
examples: She has an uncanny ability to guess what people are thinking.
The resemblance between the twins is uncanny.
His feel for the market is even more uncanny than his boss's.

entries.meaning: Not interested in other people's feelings or troubles. ---
examples: The nurse came across as cold and uncaring.
He isn't uncaring — he just doesn't know what to say.

entries.meaning: Not sorted into any group or category yet. ---

entries.meaning: Going on and on without stopping. ---

entries.meaning: Printed, shown or said with nothing cut out. ---

senses.head: Not known or not settled, and likely to change

entries.meaning: Not questioned, argued with or competed against. ---

examples: He proved unequal to the task.
The old bridge was unequal to the traffic.

entries.takes: to + noun, in sense 2 (unequal to the task)

entries.meaning: Better or greater than anything else of its kind. ---
examples: Her record of seven titles remains unequaled.
The museum has an unequaled collection of Mayan art.
He wrote with an unequaled eye for detail.
entries.position: both — often after the noun: a record unequaled in baseball
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: unequaled, unrivaled, unparalleled. British writing doubles it: unequalled.

entries.meaning: Leaving no room for doubt; completely clear. ---
examples: The answer was an unequivocal no.
Scientists are unequivocal on this point.
She gave the plan her unequivocal support.
entries.contrast: The adverb unequivocally (uhn-i-KWIV-uh-kuh-lee) is the form you meet most often: He unequivocally denied it.

entries.meaning: Against accepted standards of right behavior, especially in a profession. ---
examples: It would be unethical for a lawyer to represent both sides.
The paper accused the firm of unethical business practices.
Doctors face discipline for unethical conduct.
entries.contrast: Unethical is about professional or moral standards, illegal about the law. Plenty of things are unethical but perfectly legal.

entries.meaning: Uneven has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Watch your step — the sidewalk is uneven.
The old floor is uneven in the corners.
She tripped on the uneven pavement.
The album is uneven — two great songs and a lot of filler.
His play this season has been uneven.
It was an uneven contest from the start.
The workload is uneven across the team.

senses.head: Not flat or smooth
examples: Watch your step — the sidewalk is uneven.
The old floor is uneven in the corners.
She tripped on the uneven pavement.

senses.head: Not the same all the way through; varying in quality
examples: The album is uneven — two great songs and a lot of filler.
His play this season has been uneven.

senses.head: Not equal; one-sided
examples: It was an uneven contest from the start.
The workload is uneven across the team.

entries.contrast: For numbers Americans say odd, not uneven: an odd number.

entries.meaning: With nothing unusual or exciting happening — often a good thing. ---
examples: The flight was long but uneventful.
We had an uneventful week at the lake.
Her recovery has been thankfully uneventful.

entries.meaning: Ordinary; not especially good or interesting. ---
examples: The food was decent but unexceptional.
He was an unexceptional student who became a great teacher.
It is an unexceptional house on an unexceptional street.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with unexceptionable, a rare formal word meaning 'that nobody could object to'.

entries.meaning: Dull; not interesting or thrilling. ---
examples: It is a safe, unexciting investment.
The game was scoreless and unexciting.
My weekend was pleasant but unexciting.

entries.meaning: Not planned for; coming as a surprise. ---
examples: We had an unexpected visitor last night.
The repair bill was an unexpected 400 dollars.
His answer was unexpected, to say the least.
entries.contrast: The adverb is unexpectedly (He died unexpectedly), and the unexpected works as a noun: Be ready for the unexpected.

entries.meaning: Impossible to explain. ---
examples: For some unexplainable reason, I said yes.
The pain was unexplainable — no test showed anything.
There is something unexplainable about that house.
entries.contrast: Inexplicable means the same thing and is the commoner word in writing; unexplainable is the plainer, more spoken one.

entries.meaning: Without a known cause or reason; still not accounted for. ---
examples: The death remains unexplained.
She has been out for two weeks for unexplained reasons.
There were unexplained charges on the card.
entries.contrast: Unexplained means nobody has explained it yet; unexplainable means nobody ever could.

entries.meaning: Unexplored has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Parts of the cave system are still unexplored.
The deep ocean is largely unexplored.
That is an unexplored option.
The idea went unexplored for years.

senses.head: Not yet traveled through or mapped
examples: Parts of the cave system are still unexplored.
The deep ocean is largely unexplored.

senses.head: Not yet thought about or looked into
examples: That is an unexplored option.
The idea went unexplored for years.

entries.meaning: Always there; never running out or letting you down. ---
examples: Thank you for your unfailing support.
She met every crisis with unfailing good humor.
He had an unfailing eye for talent.
entries.position: attributive only — unfailing support, unfailing good humor

entries.meaning: Not right or just; treating people unequally. ---
examples: It is unfair to blame the teachers for this.
He got fired for something he did not do — it is completely unfair.
They gained an unfair advantage.
entries.contrast: The preposition is to, not for: That is unfair to your sister. Unfair covers both Russian несправедливый and нечестный; in a game, cheating is cheating, not unfair play.

entries.meaning: Having a romantic or sexual relationship with someone other than your partner. ---
examples: He was unfaithful to her for years.
She found out that he had been unfaithful.
An unfaithful spouse is still the reason most often given.
entries.contrast: Unfaithful is almost always about marriage or a couple; for friends and promises say disloyal. The everyday phrase is cheat on someone: He cheated on his wife.

entries.meaning: Unfamiliar has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She woke up in an unfamiliar room.
The name was unfamiliar to me.
He sang in a language unfamiliar to most of the audience.
I am unfamiliar with that software.
For readers unfamiliar with the case, here is a summary.

senses.head: Not known to you; strange
examples: She woke up in an unfamiliar room.
The name was unfamiliar to me.
He sang in a language unfamiliar to most of the audience.

senses.head: Not knowing much about something
examples: I am unfamiliar with that software.
For readers unfamiliar with the case, here is a summary.

entries.takes: to + person (it is new to them); with + noun (they do not know it)
entries.contrast: Watch the preposition: a thing is unfamiliar to a person, but a person is unfamiliar with a thing — The street was unfamiliar to me / I was unfamiliar with the street.

entries.meaning: Too strange, too deep or too large to be understood. ---
examples: The loss is unfathomable to anyone who has not lived it.
For unfathomable reasons, the city cut the bus line.
The scale of the universe is unfathomable.
entries.form: un- + fathomable, from fathom 'to measure the depth of'

entries.meaning: Unfavorable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The book got unfavorable reviews.
His poll numbers are unfavorable in every age group.
The weather was unfavorable for launch.
They sold at an unfavorable exchange rate.

senses.head: Showing disapproval; negative
examples: The book got unfavorable reviews.
His poll numbers are unfavorable in every age group.

senses.head: Not good for your plans; working against you
examples: The weather was unfavorable for launch.
They sold at an unfavorable exchange rate.

entries.contrast: American spelling drops the u: unfavorable, not unfavourable.

entries.meaning: Free from limits or control. ---
examples: The law gives the agency unfettered access to the records.
He wanted unfettered freedom to write what he liked.
Markets are rarely unfettered by regulation.
entries.position: both — before a noun, or after a verb with by

entries.meaning: Still empty or still open — of a job, a seat or an order. ---
examples: The district has 200 unfilled teaching jobs.
Her prescription sat unfilled for a week.
Half the seats on the board are unfilled.

entries.meaning: Unfinished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He left an unfinished novel on his desk.
My dinner sat unfinished.
We still have some unfinished business.
They sell unfinished pine bookcases.
The attic is still unfinished.

senses.head: Not completed
examples: He left an unfinished novel on his desk.
My dinner sat unfinished.
We still have some unfinished business.

senses.head: Of wood or furniture: not painted, stained or varnished
examples: They sell unfinished pine bookcases.
The attic is still unfinished.

entries.contrast: An unfinished basement in American real estate is one with bare concrete and no walls or flooring — a selling point in the price, not a defect.

entries.meaning: Unfit has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The water was declared unfit to drink.
A judge found him unfit to stand trial.
The building is unfit for human habitation.
I was too unfit to finish the hike.
Years at a desk left him unfit.

senses.head: Not good enough or not suitable for something
examples: The water was declared unfit to drink.
A judge found him unfit to stand trial.
The building is unfit for human habitation.

senses.head: Not in good physical condition
examples: I was too unfit to finish the hike.
Years at a desk left him unfit.

entries.contrast: For the second sense Americans usually say out of shape; unfit meaning 'not in condition' is mainly British.

entries.meaning: Staying calm no matter what happens. ---
examples: Our pediatrician is completely unflappable.
She is the unflappable type — nothing rattles her.
He was unflappable under cross-examination.
entries.form: un- + flappable, from get into a flap 'to panic'

entries.meaning: Unflattering has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It is an unflattering photo — the lighting was terrible.
Those pants are unflattering on everybody.
The article paints an unflattering picture of the mayor.
He made some unflattering comparisons.

senses.head: Making someone look worse than they really do
examples: It is an unflattering photo — the lighting was terrible.
Those pants are unflattering on everybody.

senses.head: Showing someone in a bad light; not complimentary
examples: The article paints an unflattering picture of the mayor.
He made some unflattering comparisons.

entries.meaning: Not turning away from something hard or ugly; steady and brave. ---
examples: The film is an unflinching look at addiction.
She answered with unflinching honesty.
He showed unflinching loyalty to his friends.
entries.position: attributive only — unflinching honesty, an unflinching look

entries.meaning: Unfocused has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The campaign was unfocused and lost badly.
I have been tired and unfocused all week.
The background is deliberately unfocused.
Her eyes were unfocused.

senses.head: Without a clear aim; not concentrating
examples: The campaign was unfocused and lost badly.
I have been tired and unfocused all week.

senses.head: Blurry; not sharp
examples: The background is deliberately unfocused.
Her eyes were unfocused.

entries.contrast: American English spells it with one s: focused, unfocused; British writing often doubles it.

entries.meaning: Unforced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She made 42 unforced errors.
The loss came down to unforced errors in the last set.
The movie has an unforced charm.
There was an easy, unforced warmth to his singing.

senses.head: In sports, of a mistake: caused by the player, not by the opponent
examples: She made 42 unforced errors.
The loss came down to unforced errors in the last set.

senses.head: Natural; not done under pressure
examples: The movie has an unforced charm.
There was an easy, unforced warmth to his singing.

entries.position: attributive only — an unforced error, unforced charm
entries.contrast: Unforced error has moved out of tennis into politics and business: The resignation was an unforced error.

entries.meaning: Not expected or predicted. ---
examples: The event was canceled due to unforeseen circumstances.
There were unforeseen delays at the border.
Every fix brings unforeseen problems.
entries.position: attributive only — unforeseen circumstances, unforeseen consequences

entries.meaning: So striking that you will always remember it. ---
examples: It was an unforgettable trip.
Her performance was unforgettable.
The smell of that kitchen is unforgettable.

entries.meaning: So bad that it cannot be excused. ---
examples: What he said to her was unforgivable.
Missing your own daughter's wedding would be unforgivable.
It was an unforgivable lapse in judgment.
entries.contrast: Unforgivable judges the act; unforgiving describes a person or a thing that shows no mercy.

entries.meaning: Unforgiving has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The schedule is unforgiving.
It is unforgiving terrain, all rock and ice.
Video is an unforgiving medium.
He is an unforgiving man.
She can be unforgiving when you let her down.

senses.head: Harsh; leaving no room for mistakes
examples: The schedule is unforgiving.
It is unforgiving terrain, all rock and ice.
Video is an unforgiving medium.

senses.head: Not willing to forgive people
examples: He is an unforgiving man.
She can be unforgiving when you let her down.

entries.meaning: Unfortunate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was an unfortunate choice of words.
The timing was unfortunate.
There was an unfortunate mix-up with the tickets.
Some unfortunate soul has to clean this up.
He was unfortunate enough to be standing right there.

senses.head: Regrettable; turning out in a way you wish it had not
examples: It was an unfortunate choice of words.
The timing was unfortunate.
There was an unfortunate mix-up with the tickets.

senses.head: Having bad luck
examples: Some unfortunate soul has to clean this up.
He was unfortunate enough to be standing right there.

entries.contrast: Unfortunately at the head of a sentence is the everyday way to soften bad news: Unfortunately, we cannot refund that.

entries.meaning: Not based on facts or evidence. ---
examples: The rumors turned out to be unfounded.
He made unfounded accusations against his neighbor.
Her fears were not unfounded.

entries.meaning: Not warm or welcoming toward people. ---
examples: The waiter was not rude, just unfriendly.
It is a beautiful town with an unfriendly streak.
The new manager is even unfriendlier than the last one.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — unfriendlier, unfriendliest; also more unfriendly
entries.contrast: At the end of a compound, -friendly means 'good for' or 'easy for' (kid-friendly, user-friendly); its opposite is written with a hyphen too: an environmentally unfriendly plastic.

entries.meaning: Unfulfilled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was well paid and completely unfulfilled.
She felt unfulfilled after the kids left home.
It is another unfulfilled campaign promise.
So much of his talent went unfulfilled.

senses.head: Not satisfied with your life or your work
examples: He was well paid and completely unfulfilled.
She felt unfulfilled after the kids left home.

senses.head: Not carried out or not achieved — of a promise, a hope or potential
examples: It is another unfulfilled campaign promise.
So much of his talent went unfulfilled.

entries.meaning: With no money set aside to pay for it. ---
examples: Congress keeps passing unfunded mandates.
The state has billions in unfunded pension liabilities.
The program is popular but still unfunded.

entries.meaning: Meant to be funny but not. ---
examples: The monologue was long and unfunny.
He tells the same unfunny joke every year.
It was an unfunny comedy about a funny subject.

entries.meaning: Rented with no furniture in it. ---
examples: The apartment is unfurnished.
We are looking for an unfurnished two-bedroom.
Unfurnished units rent for a few hundred less.

entries.meaning: Dull and ordinary; not exciting or attractive. ---
examples: Most of police work is unglamorous paperwork.
It is an unglamorous job, but somebody has to do it.
The town is unglamorous and cheap to live in.
entries.contrast: The noun keeps the u (glamour), but the adjective drops it in American spelling: glamorous, unglamorous.

entries.meaning: Ungodly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He calls at some ungodly hour every Sunday.
They spent an ungodly amount of money on the wedding.
The preacher warned the young people against ungodly music.
They thought the whole city led an ungodly life.

senses.head: Outrageous — unreasonably early, loud or large. Informal
examples: He calls at some ungodly hour every Sunday.
They spent an ungodly amount of money on the wedding.

senses.head: Not religious; wicked
examples: The preacher warned the young people against ungodly music.
They thought the whole city led an ungodly life.

entries.position: attributive only — an ungodly hour, an ungodly amount

entries.meaning: Breaking the rules of grammar. ---
examples: 'He don't know' is ungrammatical in standard English.
The sentence is ungrammatical, but everybody says it.
Her essay had several ungrammatical sentences.

entries.meaning: Not showing thanks for what you have been given. ---
examples: I do not want to sound ungrateful, but I wanted the blue one.
He was ungrateful for everything they did.
She called him a spoiled, ungrateful kid.

entries.meaning: Unguarded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: In an unguarded moment he admitted it.
One unguarded comment cost him the job.
The back gate was left unguarded.
Nothing at the site is unguarded at night.

senses.head: Careless; said without thinking — of a moment or a remark
examples: In an unguarded moment he admitted it.
One unguarded comment cost him the job.

senses.head: Not protected or watched
examples: The back gate was left unguarded.
Nothing at the site is unguarded at night.

entries.position: both — sense 1 only before a noun

entries.meaning: Unhappy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She had an unhappy childhood.
He looked unhappy all evening.
I have never seen her unhappier than she was that winter.
Customers are unhappy about the new fee.
The coach was unhappy with the effort.
It was an unhappy coincidence.
The whole project came to an unhappy end.

senses.head: Sad; not happy
examples: She had an unhappy childhood.
He looked unhappy all evening.
I have never seen her unhappier than she was that winter.

senses.head: Not satisfied or pleased with something
examples: Customers are unhappy about the new fee.
The coach was unhappy with the effort.

senses.head: Unlucky or badly chosen — of an event or a decision
examples: It was an unhappy coincidence.
The whole project came to an unhappy end.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — unhappier, unhappiest; also more unhappy

entries.meaning: Not hurt or damaged at all. ---
examples: The children were found unharmed.
He walked away unharmed.
The painting came through the fire unharmed.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: escaped unharmed; before a noun use uninjured

entries.meaning: Unhealthy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Fried food every day is unhealthy.
The air in the valley is unhealthier in August.
He has a lot of unhealthy habits.
The plant looks unhealthy.
She had an unhealthy gray color.
He has an unhealthy obsession with the case.
It was an unhealthy relationship from the start.

senses.head: Bad for your health
examples: Fried food every day is unhealthy.
The air in the valley is unhealthier in August.
He has a lot of unhealthy habits.

senses.head: Not in good health; looking sick
examples: The plant looks unhealthy.
She had an unhealthy gray color.

senses.head: Not normal or not good for you — of an interest or a relationship
examples: He has an unhealthy obsession with the case.
It was an unhealthy relationship from the start.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — unhealthier, unhealthiest; also more unhealthy

entries.meaning: So unusual that it has never happened before. ---
examples: A rookie winning the title was unheard-of.
They paid an unheard-of price for the house.
Snow in May is not unheard-of here.
entries.position: both — before a noun (an unheard-of price) or after a verb (It is not unheard-of)
entries.contrast: Keep the hyphen before a noun (an unheard-of delay); after a verb both unheard of and unheard-of are written.

entries.meaning: Not useful, or not willing to help. ---
examples: The support line was polite but unhelpful.
That is an unhelpful way to frame the question.
He was being deliberately unhelpful.

entries.meaning: Arriving or succeeding with no advance attention or praise. ---
examples: An unheralded rookie won the starting job.
The unheralded album became a classic.
She spent years doing unheralded work behind the scenes.

entries.meaning: Mentally unbalanced; wildly irrational. ---
examples: The email was completely unhinged.
He sounded unhinged on the phone.
It was the most unhinged thing I have ever watched.
entries.form: un- + hinged — the picture is a door off its hinges

entries.meaning: Unholy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kitchen was an unholy mess.
They made an unholy racket until two in the morning.
The two parties formed an unholy alliance.
Unholy practices were denounced from the pulpit.

senses.head: Shockingly bad or shockingly great. Informal, in fixed phrases
examples: The kitchen was an unholy mess.
They made an unholy racket until two in the morning.

senses.head: Wicked; not sacred
examples: The two parties formed an unholy alliance.
Unholy practices were denounced from the pulpit.

entries.position: attributive only — an unholy mess, an unholy alliance

entries.meaning: Dirty in a way that can spread disease. ---
examples: The kitchen was closed for unhygienic conditions.
Sharing a razor is unhygienic.
Inspectors called the whole plant unhygienic.
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech the usual word is unsanitary: unsanitary conditions.

entries.meaning: Impossible to recognize or to name. ---
examples: There was an unidentifiable smell in the fridge.
The remains were unidentifiable without dental records.
He was playing some unidentifiable instrument.

entries.meaning: Whose name or nature is not yet known. ---
examples: Police are looking for an unidentified man in a red jacket.
The victim remains unidentified.
An unidentified source told the paper about the deal.

entries.meaning: Joined into one; working as a single whole. ---
examples: We need a unified response from the states.
The company moved to a unified billing system.
The party is more unified than it looks from outside.
entries.contrast: In California and several other states a unified school district is one that runs both the elementary and the high schools.

entries.meaning: The same everywhere and at every moment; not varying. ---
examples: Cut the vegetables into uniform pieces.
The rules are not uniform across the country.
Bake it until the color is uniform.
entries.contrast: The noun is far commoner (a school uniform, in uniform); as an adjective the word is formal or technical. The adverb uniformly is frequent: uniformly excellent reviews.

entries.meaning: Wearing a uniform, especially a police or military one. ---
examples: Two uniformed officers came to the door.
Uniformed security stood at every entrance.
The parade was led by uniformed veterans.
entries.contrast: One letter apart from uninformed, which means 'knowing nothing about it': a uniformed officer is in uniform, an uninformed officer has not been told.

entries.meaning: Done by one side alone, without agreement from the others. ---
examples: The president took unilateral action.
They announced a unilateral ceasefire.
It was a unilateral decision, and nobody else was consulted.
entries.position: attributive only — a unilateral decision, unilateral action
entries.contrast: Compare bilateral (two sides) and multilateral (many). The adverb unilaterally is common: They unilaterally changed the terms.

entries.meaning: Too extreme or too strange to picture. ---
examples: The families have suffered unimaginable loss.
Such wealth was unimaginable to my grandparents.
Ten years ago this would have been unimaginable.

entries.meaning: Dull; showing no new ideas. ---
examples: The menu is safe and unimaginative.

He is careful but unimaginative.

entries.meaning: Not blocked or slowed by anything. ---
examples: The river runs unimpeded to the sea.
Aid trucks now have unimpeded access.
He rose through the ranks unimpeded by scandal.
entries.position: both — before a noun, or after a verb with by

entries.meaning: Not mattering much. ---
examples: The details are unimportant right now.
He felt small and unimportant at the meeting.
It is an unimportant game on paper.

entries.meaning: Not thinking much of something you have seen or heard. ---
examples: The judge was unimpressed by that argument.
My kids were unimpressed with the fancy hotel.
She listened and looked thoroughly unimpressed.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: was unimpressed
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with thoroughly, distinctly or singularly

entries.meaning: Not good enough to impress anyone. ---
examples: His numbers this season are unimpressive.
It is an unimpressive building from the outside.
The demo was short and unimpressive.

entries.meaning: Unincorporated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They live in an unincorporated part of the county.
The fire started on unincorporated land.
It is an unincorporated nonprofit run by volunteers.
An unincorporated business gives the owner no liability protection.

senses.head: Of land: outside the limits of any city or town, so the county governs it
examples: They live in an unincorporated part of the county.
The fire started on unincorporated land.

senses.head: Of a business or group: not legally registered as a corporation
examples: It is an unincorporated nonprofit run by volunteers.
An unincorporated business gives the owner no liability protection.

entries.русский: не входящий в черту города; не зарегистрированный как корпорация
entries.position: attributive only — unincorporated Los Angeles County

entries.meaning: Not knowing the facts about something. ---
examples: Voters should not have to make an uninformed choice.
He is completely uninformed about how the system works.
That is an uninformed opinion, not a fact.
entries.contrast: Uninformed is not uniformed (wearing a uniform), and not misinformed, which means you were told the wrong thing.

entries.meaning: Impossible to live in. ---
examples: The fire left the building uninhabitable.
Parts of the coast may become uninhabitable.
The inspector declared the apartment uninhabitable.
entries.contrast: Inhabitable means the same as habitable — fit to live in — so the in- there is not a negative. The negative word is uninhabitable.

entries.meaning: With nobody living there. ---
examples: They landed on an uninhabited island.
The house had been uninhabited for years.
Most of the region is uninhabited.

entries.meaning: Free and open in the way you behave; not shy or held back. ---
examples: She is an uninhibited dancer.
Two drinks in, he gets loud and uninhibited.
The show is famous for its uninhibited humor.

entries.meaning: Dull and ordinary; showing no spark. ---
examples: The cooking was competent but uninspired.
It was an uninspired performance.
The new logo looks uninspired.
entries.contrast: Uninspired describes work with no spark in it; uninspiring describes a thing that gives you no spark: an uninspired performance by a tired band, an uninspiring menu that leaves you cold.

entries.meaning: Not exciting or encouraging anyone. ---
examples: It was an uninspiring start to the season.
The choices on the ballot are uninspiring.
He gave a flat, uninspiring talk.

entries.meaning: Uninsured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Millions of Americans are still uninsured.
An uninsured driver hit her car.
The flood damage was uninsured.
They face thousands of dollars in uninsured losses.

senses.head: Of a person: having no health or car insurance
examples: Millions of Americans are still uninsured.
An uninsured driver hit her car.

senses.head: Of property or a loss: not covered by insurance
examples: The flood damage was uninsured.
They face thousands of dollars in uninsured losses.

entries.meaning: Impossible to understand or to make out. ---
examples: The recording is unintelligible in places.
His speech was slurred and unintelligible.
The form is unintelligible to anyone but a lawyer.

entries.meaning: Not planned or not meant to happen. ---
examples: The law had unintended consequences.
There was an unintended pause that got the biggest laugh.
Any resemblance to real people is unintended.

entries.meaning: Not done on purpose. ---
examples: The insult was unintentional, but it still stung.
It was an unintentional slip.
Any errors in the list are unintentional.
entries.contrast: The adverb unintentionally is the common form: I unintentionally left her off the list.

entries.meaning: Not holding your attention; dull. ---
examples: The first half of the book is uninteresting.
He found the whole subject uninteresting.
It is a technically uninteresting problem.
entries.contrast: Uninteresting is the thing; uninterested is the person (He was uninterested in the offer). Disinterested is a third word: it means 'having nothing to gain' — a disinterested judge, not a bored one.

entries.meaning: Going on without a break, or not blocked by anything. ---
examples: I need two uninterrupted hours to finish this.

He slept uninterrupted for ten hours.
entries.position: both — before a noun, or after a verb: She worked uninterrupted

entries.meaning: Coming or given without being asked for. ---
examples: An uninvited guest showed up with a six-pack.
He walked in uninvited.
She is tired of uninvited advice about her kids.
entries.position: both — before a noun, or after a verb: showed up uninvited

entries.meaning: Belonging to a labor union — of workers or of a workplace. ---
examples: The plant is fully unionized.
Unionized workers earn about 15 percent more on average.
Only one of their stores is unionized.
entries.contrast: American English writes unionize, unionized with a z; the -ise spelling is British.

entries.meaning: Made for both men and women. ---
examples: The gym has a unisex locker room.
It is a unisex fragrance.
The shirts come in unisex sizes only.

entries.meaning: United has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A united Germany came in 1990.
They campaigned for a united Ireland.
The family is united in its grief.
The party is more united than it was a year ago.

senses.head: Joined together into one country, group or organization
examples: A united Germany came in 1990.
They campaigned for a united Ireland.

senses.head: In agreement; acting together
examples: The family is united in its grief.
The party is more united than it was a year ago.

entries.takes: in + noun or -ing, in sense 2 (united in grief)
entries.contrast: Capitalized in names: the United States, the United Nations, the United Kingdom.

entries.meaning: Not fair or right — especially of a law, a system or a punishment. ---
examples: They call the sentence unjust.
He spent his life fighting an unjust system.
Nothing is more unjust than punishing the wrong person.
entries.contrast: Unjust is formal and belongs to laws, rulings and systems; for everyday complaints say unfair: It is unfair that she got a bigger piece.

entries.meaning: Impossible to defend with any good reason. ---
examples: The delay is unjustifiable.
He called the spending unjustifiable.
It was an unjustifiable use of force.

entries.meaning: Not supported by a good reason; not deserved. ---
examples: The fear turned out to be unjustified.
She complained about unjustified charges on the bill.
His confidence was entirely unjustified.
entries.contrast: Unjustified says there was no good reason for it this time; unjustifiable says there could never be one.

entries.meaning: Messy and not taken care of, said of hair, clothes or a yard. ---
examples: He showed up for the interview in an unkempt suit.
Her hair was unkempt and her eyes were red.
The yard grew more unkempt every week the family was away.
entries.form: un- + kempt, an old participle meaning combed

entries.meaning: Saying or doing things that hurt people. ---
examples: It was unkind of you to laugh at her accent.
Don't be unkind to your little brother.
That was the unkindest thing anyone has ever said to me.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — unkinder, unkindest; also more unkind, most unkind

entries.meaning: Not aware of what is really going on. ---
examples: The scam used unknowing students to move the money.
She was an unknowing witness to the whole argument.
Tourists make unknowing mistakes that the locals find funny.
entries.contrast: Unknowing describes the person who doesn't realize; the adverb unknowingly describes the act: he unknowingly signed away his rights.

entries.meaning: Having no label or name on it. ---
examples: There were three unlabeled jars at the back of the fridge.
Never open an unlabeled file from a stranger.
Half the boxes in the garage are still unlabeled.
entries.contrast: American English writes one l: unlabeled. British books print unlabelled.

entries.meaning: Against the law. ---
examples: The court found the search unlawful.
He was charged with unlawful possession of a firearm.
Firing someone for reporting a safety problem is unlawful.
entries.contrast: Illegal is the everyday word. Unlawful belongs to legal language and to fixed phrases: unlawful entry, unlawful detention.

entries.meaning: Made without added lead, said of gasoline. ---
examples: Most cars built after 1975 need unleaded gas.
The station sells three grades of unleaded fuel.
Older engines were never designed to run on unleaded gasoline.
entries.form: un- + leaded, from lead the metal
entries.contrast: The lead here is the metal, said like led, so the word rhymes with shredded. At the pump Americans also use it as a noun: fill it up with unleaded.

entries.meaning: Without the official permit the law requires. ---
examples: An unlicensed contractor did the wiring, and it shows.
The city shut down two unlicensed day care centers.
Practicing medicine while unlicensed is a felony.
entries.contrast: American English spells both the noun and the verb license, so the adjective is unlicensed; British English writes the noun licence.

entries.meaning: Hard to like. ---
examples: Every character in the novel is unlikable in a different way.
He isn't evil, just unlikable.
The remake made the hero more unlikable than the villain.
entries.contrast: American English drops the e: likable, unlikable. Unlikeable is the British spelling.

entries.meaning: With no limit on the amount, the number or the time. ---
examples: The plan comes with unlimited texting.
Kids get unlimited refills at that diner.
Your access to the archive is unlimited for a year.

entries.meaning: Unlisted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her number is unlisted, so you'll have to email her.
The house is unlisted, which is why it never came up in my search.
I made the video unlisted so only the family can watch it.
Unlisted posts don't show up in search results.

senses.head: Kept out of a public directory or list
examples: Her number is unlisted, so you'll have to email her.
The house is unlisted, which is why it never came up in my search.

senses.head: Visible only to people who have the link, said of a video or a page
body: (доступный только по ссылке, скрытый из поиска)
examples: I made the video unlisted so only the family can watch it.
Unlisted posts don't show up in search results.

entries.русский: не внесённый в справочник; доступный только по ссылке
entries.contrast: An unlisted phone number is one the phone company keeps out of the directory; the British term is ex-directory.

entries.meaning: Unlit has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't walk home down that unlit alley.
The parking lot is unlit after midnight.
An unlit cigarette hung from his mouth.
The birthday candles were still unlit when we started singing.

senses.head: Having no lights; dark
examples: Don't walk home down that unlit alley.
The parking lot is unlit after midnight.

senses.head: Not burning, said of a candle or a cigarette
examples: An unlit cigarette hung from his mouth.
The birthday candles were still unlit when we started singing.

entries.form: un- + lit, the past participle of light

entries.meaning: Impossible, or almost impossible, to live in. ---
examples: The mold made the apartment unlivable.
Rents like these make the city unlivable for teachers.
Every August the top floor gets more unlivable.
entries.contrast: American English drops the e: livable, unlivable. British books print unliveable.

entries.meaning: Unlocked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She left the back door unlocked again.
An unlocked bike downtown won't last an hour.
I bought an unlocked phone so I could switch plans.
Is the phone unlocked, or is it still on a contract?

senses.head: Not fastened with a lock
examples: She left the back door unlocked again.
An unlocked bike downtown won't last an hour.

senses.head: Not tied to one carrier, said of a phone
examples: I bought an unlocked phone so I could switch plans.
Is the phone unlocked, or is it still on a contract?

entries.meaning: Getting no love or affection from anyone. ---
examples: No child should grow up feeling unloved.
The old piano sat unloved in the corner of the basement.
He felt more unloved after the divorce than he ever had as a kid.

entries.meaning: Unlucky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We were unlucky with the weather all week.
She was unlucky to hit every red light on Main Street.
He is the unluckiest driver I know.
Some hotels skip the thirteenth floor because the number is unlucky.
My grandmother thinks it's unlucky to open an umbrella indoors.

senses.head: Having bad luck
examples: We were unlucky with the weather all week.
She was unlucky to hit every red light on Main Street.
He is the unluckiest driver I know.

senses.head: Believed to bring bad luck
examples: Some hotels skip the thirteenth floor because the number is unlucky.
My grandmother thinks it's unlucky to open an umbrella indoors.

entries.meaning: Not straightened out after being slept in, said of a bed. ---
examples: He left for work with an unmade bed, as usual.
The camera panned across a messy room and an unmade bed.
Housekeeping never leaves an unmade bed behind.
entries.position: both — an unmade bed is far more common than the bed is unmade
entries.contrast: It goes with beds and almost nothing else. For a room that hasn't been tidied, say the room is a mess, not the room is unmade.

entries.meaning: Too big, too difficult or too wild to control. ---
examples: My hair gets unmanageable in humid weather.
The class became unmanageable the minute the substitute walked in.
The debt grew more unmanageable every month.

entries.meaning: Working with nobody on board or on duty. ---
examples: An unmanned aircraft photographed the fire.
The gate is unmanned after six, so bring your badge.
NASA sent several unmanned probes to Mars first.
entries.contrast: Uncrewed is now preferred at NASA and in science writing, but an unmanned drone is still what you hear on the news.

entries.meaning: Carrying no sign, label or markings that would identify it. ---
examples: An unmarked police car pulled us over.
The trail is unmarked past the river, so bring a map.
They buried him in an unmarked grave.

entries.meaning: Not married. ---
examples: Both of my uncles are unmarried.
The form asks whether you are married or unmarried.
An unmarried couple bought the house next door.
entries.contrast: Forms and conversation usually offer single. Unmarried is the more formal word and the one used in an unmarried couple living together.

entries.meaning: Unmatched has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her record in the 400 meters is still unmatched.
The view from the top of the ridge is unmatched.
He wore two unmatched socks to school.
There is a whole drawer of unmatched gloves by the door.

senses.head: Better than anything else of its kind
examples: Her record in the 400 meters is still unmatched.
The view from the top of the ridge is unmatched.

senses.head: Not forming a pair
examples: He wore two unmatched socks to school.
There is a whole drawer of unmatched gloves by the door.

entries.contrast: For socks and shoes Americans usually say mismatched. On its own, unmatched almost always means better than all the rest.

entries.meaning: So clear that you cannot be wrong about it. ---
examples: There was an unmistakable smell of gas in the hallway.
Her handwriting is unmistakable.
The look on his face was unmistakable — he had forgotten.
entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: the final e of mistake drops out — unmistakable, not unmistakeable.

entries.meaning: Complete, with nothing to soften it. ---
examples: Opening night was an unmitigated disaster.
Calling the merger an unmitigated failure is putting it kindly.
What he wrote in that letter was unmitigated nonsense.
entries.position: attributive only — an unmitigated disaster, never the disaster was unmitigated
entries.form: un- + mitigated, from mitigate 'to make less severe'
entries.contrast: It nearly always sits in front of a bad noun: an unmitigated disaster, an unmitigated failure, unmitigated nonsense.

entries.meaning: Having no desire to work or make an effort. ---
examples: By March the whole class was tired and unmotivated.
He isn't lazy, just unmotivated by this particular job.
Working from home left her more unmotivated than she expected.

entries.meaning: Feeling no emotion or pity about something. ---
examples: The jury seemed unmoved by his apology.
She listened to the whole story unmoved.
Voters were unmoved by the last-minute ads.
entries.position: predicative only — she was unmoved, not an unmoved judge

entries.meaning: Whose name is not given. ---
examples: Two unnamed officials confirmed the story.
The money came from an unnamed donor.
The buyer wishes to stay unnamed.
entries.position: both — usually before a noun: an unnamed source

entries.meaning: Unnatural has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The room was filled with an unnatural silence.
Eighty degrees in February feels unnatural.
His laugh sounded unnatural on camera.
She held the smile so long that it looked unnatural.
Reading from a script makes some people sound more unnatural than they really are.

senses.head: Not normal; going against the way things usually are
examples: The room was filled with an unnatural silence.
Eighty degrees in February feels unnatural.

senses.head: Forced; not the way a person really behaves
examples: His laugh sounded unnatural on camera.
She held the smile so long that it looked unnatural.
Reading from a script makes some people sound more unnatural than they really are.

entries.meaning: Not needed. ---
examples: The surgery turned out to be unnecessary.
You made an unnecessary trip — I could have emailed it.
All that shouting was completely unnecessary.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely or totally
entries.contrast: Russian speakers often reach for needless. Unnecessary is the everyday word; needless survives mainly in needless to say.

entries.meaning: Not seen or noticed by anyone. ---
examples: The typo went unnoticed until the book was printed.
She slipped out of the party unnoticed.
A leak that size does not stay unnoticed for long.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always after go, pass or slip: the typo went unnoticed
entries.contrast: It lives in the pattern go unnoticed or pass unnoticed. Before a noun it sounds wrong: say a mistake nobody caught, not an unnoticed mistake.

entries.meaning: With nothing standing in the way. ---
examples: The room has an unobstructed view of the lake.
Keep the fire exit unobstructed at all times.
From row A the stage is completely unobstructed.

entries.meaning: Not attracting attention; quiet and easy to ignore. ---
examples: The security cameras are small and unobtrusive.
A good waiter is friendly but unobtrusive.
We picked the most unobtrusive table in the room.

entries.meaning: Empty; with nobody living in it or using it. ---
examples: The house has been unoccupied since spring.
Take any unoccupied seat in the back.
Two offices on that floor are still unoccupied.

entries.meaning: Not confirmed or approved by the people in charge. ---
examples: The unofficial count has her ahead by two hundred votes.
Sunday practice is unofficial, so nobody has to come.
He is the team's unofficial captain.
entries.contrast: Unofficial means not confirmed by whoever is in charge; informal means relaxed in style. An unofficial count is not yet certified; an informal dinner has no dress code.

entries.meaning: Still sealed or closed; never opened. ---
examples: There is an unopened bottle of wine in the pantry.
Her mail sat unopened for two weeks.
The store takes returns only on unopened boxes.

entries.meaning: With nobody competing against you or arguing against it. ---
examples: She ran unopposed for a second term.
The motion passed unopposed.
The bill cleared the committee unopposed.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: she ran unopposed

entries.meaning: Not arranged or planned; without any order. ---
examples: My notes for this class are completely unorganized.
The move was unorganized from the first day.
Their closet is more unorganized than mine, which is saying something.
entries.contrast: For a messy person or room, disorganized is the usual word. Unorganized is common in American speech and is the standard term for workers with no union: an unorganized workforce.

entries.meaning: Copied from, or too much like, something that already exists. ---
examples: The plot is unoriginal, but the acting is good.
My costume was unoriginal — three other people came as pirates.
Nothing is more unoriginal than a band name that starts with The.

entries.meaning: Not done the usual way. ---
examples: She has an unorthodox pitching motion that somehow works.
His teaching methods are unorthodox but effective.
The most unorthodox solution turned out to be the cheapest.
entries.contrast: Lowercase unorthodox just means done in an unusual way. Capitalized Orthodox names a church or a branch of Judaism — a different word.

entries.meaning: Unpaid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Two invoices from March are still unpaid.
They shut off the water over an unpaid bill.
She took three months of unpaid leave.
Most of the campaign staff were unpaid volunteers.

senses.head: Not yet paid, said of a bill or a debt
examples: Two invoices from March are still unpaid.
They shut off the water over an unpaid bill.

senses.head: Done without pay, said of work or leave
examples: She took three months of unpaid leave.
Most of the campaign staff were unpaid volunteers.

entries.meaning: Unpalatable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soup was cold and frankly unpalatable.
Hospital food has an unpalatable reputation.
The report contains some unpalatable facts about the school.
Both options were unpalatable, so we waited.
The longer he stalled, the more unpalatable the choices became.

senses.head: Unpleasant to eat
examples: The soup was cold and frankly unpalatable.
Hospital food has an unpalatable reputation.

senses.head: Hard to accept
examples: The report contains some unpalatable facts about the school.
Both options were unpalatable, so we waited.
The longer he stalled, the more unpalatable the choices became.

entries.form: un- + palatable, from palate 'the roof of the mouth'

entries.meaning: Greater or better than anything else of its kind. ---
examples: The museum has an unparalleled collection of Native American baskets.
She brings unparalleled energy to the job.
The storm caused damage unparalleled in the county's history.
entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: one r, two l's in the middle, one l at the end — un-par-al-leled.

entries.meaning: Not heated to kill bacteria, said of milk, juice or cheese. ---
examples: Unpasteurized milk cannot be sold across state lines.
The cheese is made from unpasteurized goat's milk.
Doctors tell pregnant women to avoid anything unpasteurized.
entries.form: un- + pasteurized, from the chemist Louis Pasteur
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ized; British books print unpasteurised.

entries.meaning: Showing no loyalty to your country, or seeming not to. ---
examples: Criticizing a war is not unpatriotic.
He was called unpatriotic for refusing to stand.
Nothing is more unpatriotic, she argued, than lying to voters.
entries.contrast: In American English the first syllable rhymes with pay: uhn-pay-tree-AH-tik. British speakers say pat- instead.

entries.meaning: Not covered with asphalt or concrete. ---
examples: The last two miles of the road are unpaved.
An unpaved driveway leads up to the cabin.
Half the streets in the old town are still unpaved.

entries.meaning: Calm; not worried or upset by what is happening. ---
examples: The cat sat unperturbed while the dog barked at it.
She was unperturbed by the boos from the crowd.
He looked unperturbed when the lights went out.

entries.meaning: Not arranged in advance; happening by chance. ---
examples: We made an unplanned stop in Memphis.
The pregnancy was unplanned but very welcome.
The best parts of the trip were all unplanned.

entries.meaning: Unplayable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Three days of rain left the field unplayable.
His ball came to rest in a bush, unplayable.
The game shipped so buggy that it was unplayable for a month.
The old DVD is scratched and unplayable.

senses.head: Impossible to play on, said of a field or a golf lie
examples: Three days of rain left the field unplayable.
His ball came to rest in a bush, unplayable.

senses.head: Impossible to play, said of a game, a disc or a recording
examples: The game shipped so buggy that it was unplayable for a month.
The old DVD is scratched and unplayable.

entries.meaning: Unpleasant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There was an unpleasant smell coming from the basement.
That flight was the most unpleasant six hours of my life.
The clerk was openly unpleasant to everyone in line.
He can be unpleasant when he hasn't slept.

senses.head: Not enjoyable; leaving you with a bad feeling
examples: There was an unpleasant smell coming from the basement.
That flight was the most unpleasant six hours of my life.

senses.head: Rude or unfriendly, said of a person
examples: The clerk was openly unpleasant to everyone in line.
He can be unpleasant when he hasn't slept.

entries.meaning: Unpolished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Unpolished floors show every scratch.
The stone is unpolished, so it looks dull until you wet it.
The draft is unpolished, but the argument is all there.
His delivery is unpolished, and audiences like him for it.
Her early songs were more unpolished and, some say, better.

senses.head: Not made smooth or shiny
examples: Unpolished floors show every scratch.
The stone is unpolished, so it looks dull until you wet it.

senses.head: Rough; not yet worked into finished shape
examples: The draft is unpolished, but the argument is all there.
His delivery is unpolished, and audiences like him for it.
Her early songs were more unpolished and, some say, better.

entries.meaning: Disliked by most people. ---
examples: The new tax was unpopular with almost everyone.
She made the unpopular decision to cancel the trip.
The mayor is more unpopular now than when she took office.

entries.meaning: Never having happened before. ---
examples: The city saw unprecedented flooding in October.
She won three titles in one year, an unprecedented run.
Demand for the vaccine was unprecedented.
entries.form: un- + precedented, from precedent 'an earlier case'
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable and the vowel is short: uhn-PRES-i-den-tid, never un-pre-SEE-.

entries.meaning: Impossible to know in advance; changing without warning. ---
examples: Mountain weather in April is unpredictable.
He is a good player but unpredictable under pressure.
The market has been more unpredictable than usual this year.

entries.meaning: Not ready for what is about to happen. ---
examples: We were completely unprepared for the cold.
He walked into the exam unprepared.
She was unprepared to answer questions about the layoffs.

entries.meaning: Simple and modest; not trying to seem important. ---
examples: It's an unpretentious little diner with very good pie.
For a famous writer he is remarkably unpretentious.
The most unpretentious house on the street is also the oldest.

entries.meaning: Willing to do wrong things to get what you want. ---
examples: An unprincipled landlord will find a way around the rule.
The whole campaign was unprincipled from the first week.
He is the most unprincipled person I have ever worked for.

entries.meaning: Unprocessed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The diet is built around unprocessed foods.
Unprocessed oats take longer to cook than instant ones.
Thousands of claims are still unprocessed.
My refund sat unprocessed for six weeks.

senses.head: Not changed from its natural state, said of food
examples: The diet is built around unprocessed foods.
Unprocessed oats take longer to cook than instant ones.

senses.head: Not yet dealt with, said of paperwork or data
examples: Thousands of claims are still unprocessed.
My refund sat unprocessed for six weeks.

entries.meaning: Producing little or nothing useful. ---
examples: The meeting was two unproductive hours.
Arguing about who is to blame is unproductive.
That was the most unproductive week I have had all year.

entries.meaning: Not meeting the standards of behavior expected at work. ---
examples: Yelling at a customer is unprofessional.
The email was unprofessional and a little cruel.
Nothing looks more unprofessional than a typo in the subject line.
entries.contrast: In American English it is almost always about behavior, not skill. Someone who does poor work is incompetent; someone who shouts at a client is unprofessional.

entries.meaning: Not making money. ---
examples: They closed three unprofitable stores.
The airline's shortest routes are the most unprofitable.
Farming that land is unprofitable without subsidies.

entries.meaning: Done without anyone asking or suggesting it. ---
examples: He offered to pay, completely unprompted.
An unprompted apology means more than one you had to ask for.
She named all fifty states unprompted.
entries.contrast: The adverb unpromptedly exists but is rare; Americans use the adjective where Russian would use an adverb: he offered to help, unprompted.

entries.meaning: Too difficult to say out loud. ---
examples: The ingredient list is full of unpronounceable chemicals.
Her last name is beautiful and, for most Americans, unpronounceable.
He gave the dog an unpronounceable Welsh name.
entries.contrast: Keep the e of pronounce before -able: pronounceable, unpronounceable.

entries.meaning: With nothing to keep it safe from harm. ---
examples: Don't leave your laptop unprotected on an open network.
The beach is unprotected from the north wind.
Unprotected seedlings won't survive a frost.

entries.meaning: Unproven has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The claim is unproven and probably false.
Unproven remedies sell very well online.
The team is starting an unproven quarterback.
They bet the company on an unproven technology.

senses.head: Not shown to be true
examples: The claim is unproven and probably false.
Unproven remedies sell very well online.

senses.head: Not yet tested in real conditions
examples: The team is starting an unproven quarterback.
They bet the company on an unproven technology.

entries.contrast: Unproven and unproved are both correct, but unproven is far more common in American writing.

entries.meaning: Happening without anything being done to cause it. ---
examples: It was an unprovoked attack on a man waiting for a bus.
The report lists six unprovoked shark encounters last year.
Her outburst was sudden and unprovoked.

entries.meaning: Not printed or made public. ---
examples: Three of her novels are still unpublished.
The library bought a box of unpublished letters.
The study remains unpublished two years after it was finished.

entries.meaning: Not punished. ---
examples: The vandalism went unpunished.
No good deed goes unpunished.
He can't let an insult go unpunished.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always after go: the crime went unpunished
entries.contrast: It lives in the pattern go unpunished. Before a noun it sounds wrong: say a crime nobody was punished for.

entries.meaning: Unqualified has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is unqualified for the job and everyone knows it.
An unqualified aide was left in charge of the class.
She is unqualified to give medical advice.
The concert was an unqualified success.
She gave the plan her unqualified support.

senses.head: Not having the training, skills or right to do something
examples: He is unqualified for the job and everyone knows it.
An unqualified aide was left in charge of the class.
She is unqualified to give medical advice.

senses.head: Complete, with nothing held back
examples: The concert was an unqualified success.
She gave the plan her unqualified support.

entries.contrast: Two almost opposite feelings. After a verb it means not trained enough: he is unqualified. Before a noun like success or support it means total: an unqualified success.

entries.meaning: Certain; impossible to doubt. ---
examples: Her talent is unquestionable.
The evidence for the link is by now unquestionable.
He has an unquestionable right to see the file.

entries.meaning: Accepting something completely, without ever asking why. ---
examples: The group demands unquestioning loyalty.
He gave the coach four years of unquestioning obedience.
Unquestioning trust in a website is how people get scammed.
entries.position: attributive only — unquestioning loyalty, unquestioning obedience
