entries.contrast: Don't mix it up with unquestionable. Unquestioning loyalty is loyalty that never asks why; unquestionable loyalty is loyalty nobody can doubt.

entries.meaning: Not among the teams or players on the official ranking list. ---
examples: An unranked team beat the number two seed.
She was unranked coming into the tournament.
The Tigers open the season unranked for the first time in years.
entries.русский: не входящий в рейтинг, без места в рейтинге

entries.meaning: Unreachable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The nest sits on an unreachable ledge.
The top shelf is unreachable without a stool.
She's unreachable until Monday morning.
The server was unreachable all afternoon.

senses.head: Impossible to get to or touch
examples: The nest sits on an unreachable ledge.
The top shelf is unreachable without a stool.

senses.head: Impossible to contact
examples: She's unreachable until Monday morning.
The server was unreachable all afternoon.

entries.meaning: Not read by anyone. ---
examples: I have four hundred unread emails.
The report sat unread on his desk for a month.
Mark all the messages as unread.
entries.contrast: Here read is the past participle, said like red: uhn-RED, never uhn-REED. The related unreadable does use the long vowel.

entries.meaning: Unreadable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His handwriting is unreadable.
The disk is damaged and unreadable.
The manual is technically accurate and completely unreadable.
It is the most unreadable book on the syllabus.

senses.head: Impossible to make out
examples: His handwriting is unreadable.
The disk is damaged and unreadable.

senses.head: Too dull or too difficult to get through
examples: The manual is technically accurate and completely unreadable.
It is the most unreadable book on the syllabus.

entries.contrast: Note the vowel change: unread is uhn-RED, but unreadable is uhn-REE-duh-buhl.

entries.meaning: Unreal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Everything about that week felt unreal.
The colors in the photo look unreal.
The view from the summit was unreal.
That catch in the ninth inning was unreal.

senses.head: Not real, or too strange to feel real
examples: Everything about that week felt unreal.
The colors in the photo look unreal.

senses.head: Amazing — informal
examples: The view from the summit was unreal.
That catch in the ninth inning was unreal.

entries.contrast: In casual American speech unreal is praise: that concert was unreal means it was fantastic.

entries.meaning: Not sensible about what is actually possible. ---
examples: The deadline is unrealistic.
It's unrealistic to expect a reply the same day.
Their budget was more unrealistic than the schedule.

entries.meaning: Unrealized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The whole article is about unrealized potential.
His plan for the park is one more unrealized dream.
You owe no tax on unrealized gains.
The fund is carrying a large unrealized loss.

senses.head: Never achieved or developed
examples: The whole article is about unrealized potential.
His plan for the park is one more unrealized dream.

senses.head: Existing on paper but not yet turned into cash, said of gains or losses
examples: You owe no tax on unrealized gains.
The fund is carrying a large unrealized loss.

entries.position: attributive only — unrealized potential, unrealized gains
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ized; British books print unrealised.

entries.meaning: Unreasonable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her boss makes unreasonable demands.
It isn't unreasonable to ask for two days' notice.
He gets more unreasonable the later the meeting runs.
They charge an unreasonable amount for parking.
The rent increase was plainly unreasonable.

senses.head: Not fair or sensible
examples: Her boss makes unreasonable demands.
It isn't unreasonable to ask for two days' notice.
He gets more unreasonable the later the meeting runs.

senses.head: Far greater than is fair, said of a price or an amount
examples: They charge an unreasonable amount for parking.
The rent increase was plainly unreasonable.

entries.meaning: So changed that you cannot tell what or who it is. ---
examples: Downtown is unrecognizable after ten years away.
He shaved his beard and was almost unrecognizable.
The fire left the car unrecognizable.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses z: unrecognizable. British books print unrecognisable.

entries.meaning: Unrecognized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The disease often goes unrecognized for years.
She walked through the hotel lobby unrecognized.
The territory is an unrecognized state.
His degree is unrecognized in the United States.

senses.head: Not noticed or identified
examples: The disease often goes unrecognized for years.
She walked through the hotel lobby unrecognized.

senses.head: Not officially accepted
examples: The territory is an unrecognized state.
His degree is unrecognized in the United States.

entries.meaning: Impossible to get back. ---
examples: The files on the burned drive are unrecoverable.
Once you empty the trash, deleted photos may be unrecoverable.
Most of that loan is unrecoverable.

entries.meaning: Unrefined has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The recipe calls for unrefined coconut oil.
Unrefined sugar keeps more of the molasses.
His humor is unrefined but never mean.
She thought their taste in furniture was unrefined.
The earlier draft was more unrefined, and funnier for it.

senses.head: Not processed; still close to its natural state
examples: The recipe calls for unrefined coconut oil.
Unrefined sugar keeps more of the molasses.

senses.head: Rough; lacking polish or good manners
examples: His humor is unrefined but never mean.
She thought their taste in furniture was unrefined.
The earlier draft was more unrefined, and funnier for it.

entries.meaning: Not entered on an official list. ---
examples: Driving an unregistered car will get you a ticket.
Thousands of eligible voters are still unregistered.
The gun turned out to be unregistered.

entries.meaning: Not controlled by government rules. ---
examples: The supplement industry is largely unregulated.
Unregulated lending helped cause the crash.
He worries about an unregulated market for these chemicals.

entries.meaning: Done without practicing it first. ---
examples: The interview was completely unrehearsed.
They gave an unrehearsed performance and it worked.
Her answer sounded unrehearsed, which is why people believed it.

entries.meaning: Unrelated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The two cases are unrelated.
She quit for reasons unrelated to the lawsuit.
On an unrelated note, did anyone fix the printer?
The two Smiths in my class are unrelated.
They share a last name but are unrelated.

senses.head: Not connected with something else
examples: The two cases are unrelated.
She quit for reasons unrelated to the lawsuit.
On an unrelated note, did anyone fix the printer?

senses.head: Not from the same family
examples: The two Smiths in my class are unrelated.
They share a last name but are unrelated.

entries.русский: не связанный; не состоящий в родстве

entries.meaning: Not yet made available to the public. ---
examples: The album includes two unreleased tracks.
Fans trade unreleased demos online.
The movie has been finished but unreleased for two years.

entries.meaning: Never stopping or getting any weaker. ---
examples: The heat in August was unrelenting.
She faced unrelenting pressure from the board.
His critics have been unrelenting.
entries.form: un- + relenting, from relent 'to give in'

entries.meaning: Not to be trusted to work, to be true, or to do what was promised. ---
examples: The bus out to the airport is unreliable.
He is a warm person but an unreliable friend.
That website is the most unreliable source on the list.

entries.meaning: Ordinary; with nothing about it worth noticing. ---
examples: From the street it's an unremarkable brick building.
The meal was pleasant and unremarkable.
He has one of the most unremarkable faces I have ever seen.

entries.meaning: Continuing without a break, usually of something hard to bear. ---
examples: Three weeks of unremitting rain flooded the fields.
The job demands unremitting attention to detail.
They lived under unremitting pressure to sell the farm.
entries.position: attributive only — unremitting pressure, unremitting rain
entries.form: un- + remitting, from remit 'to let up'
entries.contrast: Unremitting and unrelenting mean much the same thing, but unremitting is the more formal, more bookish of the two.

entries.meaning: Not sorry for something you did wrong. ---
examples: He was unrepentant at his sentencing.
She is unrepentant about the post.
The paper called him an unrepentant liar.

entries.meaning: Not told to the authorities or to the public. ---
examples: Most cases of the illness go unreported.
He had thousands of dollars in unreported income.
The crash stayed unreported for a week.

entries.meaning: Not returned, said of love or affection. ---
examples: The whole album is about unrequited love.
He spent a year on an unrequited crush.
Her affection for him was unrequited.
entries.position: both — almost always before a noun, in the phrase unrequited love
entries.form: un- + requited, from the old verb requite 'to return in kind'
entries.contrast: You will meet it in one phrase, unrequited love, and hardly anywhere else.

entries.meaning: Not settled or decided. ---
examples: The dispute is still unresolved.
There are two unresolved questions in the report.
He left the meeting with a lot of unresolved anger.

entries.meaning: Unresponsive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The agency has been unresponsive to every complaint.
He sat unresponsive through the whole meeting.
The tumor was unresponsive to chemotherapy.
The touchscreen goes unresponsive in cold weather.
Paramedics found her unresponsive on the kitchen floor.

senses.head: Not answering or reacting to people
examples: The agency has been unresponsive to every complaint.
He sat unresponsive through the whole meeting.

senses.head: Not reacting to treatment, to input, or to anything at all
examples: The tumor was unresponsive to chemotherapy.
The touchscreen goes unresponsive in cold weather.
Paramedics found her unresponsive on the kitchen floor.

entries.meaning: Not held back or kept under control. ---
examples: The crowd greeted her with unrestrained cheering.
He wrote about the trip with unrestrained joy.
Her anger that night was completely unrestrained.

entries.meaning: With no rules limiting it. ---
examples: Members get unrestricted access to the archive.
The grant money is unrestricted, so we can spend it where it's needed.
Unrestricted travel between the two countries resumed in June.

entries.meaning: Not yet ready to eat or pick. ---
examples: The peaches at the store were hard and unripe.
Unripe tomatoes are good fried.
The fruit at the bottom of the box was more unripe than the rest.

entries.meaning: Better than anything or anyone else of its kind. ---
examples: The store has an unrivaled selection of used records.
Her knowledge of the river is unrivaled.
For pure speed the train is unrivaled.
entries.contrast: American English writes one l: unrivaled. British books print unrivalled.

entries.meaning: Unruly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: An unruly fan was escorted out in the third inning.
The class got unruly right after lunch.
It was the unruliest crowd the arena had seen all year.
He pushed his unruly hair out of his eyes.
Unruly curls run in the family.

senses.head: Hard to control, said of a person or a crowd
examples: An unruly fan was escorted out in the third inning.
The class got unruly right after lunch.
It was the unruliest crowd the arena had seen all year.

senses.head: Sticking out and hard to comb, said of hair
examples: He pushed his unruly hair out of his eyes.
Unruly curls run in the family.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — unrulier, unruliest; also more unruly, most unruly
entries.contrast: It ends in -ly but it is an adjective, not an adverb — like friendly and lonely. There is no adverb unrulily; say in an unruly way.

entries.meaning: Likely to cause harm, or not protected from harm. ---
examples: The inspector closed the plant after finding unsafe conditions.
The water here is unsafe to drink.
She felt unsafe walking home after dark.
entries.position: both — unsafe working conditions, The bridge is unsafe
entries.comparison: more/most — more unsafe, most unsafe; unsafer is rare
entries.takes: for + person (unsafe for children); to-infinitive (unsafe to drink)

entries.meaning: Not said, though it could have been. ---
examples: Some things are better left unsaid.
A lot went unsaid at dinner that night.
The apology remained unsaid for twenty years.
entries.position: predicative only — after leave, go or remain: left unsaid, what went unsaid
entries.contrast: Not the same as unspoken. An unspoken rule is understood without being stated; something unsaid was simply never said, often on purpose: Some things are better left unsaid.

entries.meaning: Made or cooked without salt added. ---
examples: The recipe calls for a stick of unsalted butter.
We buy unsalted nuts for the kids.
These crackers are completely unsalted.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unsalted butter

entries.meaning: Dirty enough to be a danger to health. ---
examples: The restaurant was shut down for unsanitary conditions.
Workers were living in crowded, unsanitary housing.
Storing raw meat that way is unsanitary.
entries.contrast: American writing uses unsanitary; the British word for the same thing is insanitary.

entries.meaning: Not good enough for what is needed. ---
examples: His explanation was unsatisfactory, so we asked again.
The company gave us an unsatisfactory answer about the delay.
Two students received an unsatisfactory grade in the course.
entries.contrast: Three neighbors that learners mix up: a result is unsatisfactory (not good enough), a person is unsatisfied (not pleased), and an experience is unsatisfying (it leaves you wanting more).

entries.meaning: Unsatisfied has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Customers who are unsatisfied can return the item for a refund.
She left the meeting unsatisfied with the answers.
He was unsatisfied even after a second helping.
There is still a large unsatisfied demand for affordable housing.
The loan will not close while two conditions remain unsatisfied.

senses.head: Not pleased, because something fell short of what you wanted
examples: Customers who are unsatisfied can return the item for a refund.
She left the meeting unsatisfied with the answers.
He was unsatisfied even after a second helping.

senses.head: Not met or filled, said of a need, a demand or a condition
examples: There is still a large unsatisfied demand for affordable housing.
The loan will not close while two conditions remain unsatisfied.

entries.meaning: Leaving you wanting more; not giving a feeling of satisfaction. ---
examples: The movie had a rushed, unsatisfying ending.
A salad alone makes for an unsatisfying lunch.
After ten years the work had become unsatisfying.
entries.position: both — an unsatisfying job, The ending was unsatisfying
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling; un- + satisfying
entries.contrast: The -ing word describes the thing (an unsatisfying movie); the -ed word describes the person (I was unsatisfied).

entries.meaning: Of a fat or oil, having double bonds between carbon atoms, and so generally better for your health. ---
examples: Olive oil is high in unsaturated fat.
The label lists both unsaturated and saturated fats.
Most of the fat in walnuts is unsaturated.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unsaturated fats

entries.meaning: Not yet stored on a computer, so it can be lost. ---
examples: A warning popped up about unsaved changes.
The laptop died and an hour of unsaved work went with it.
The draft is still unsaved, so do not close the tab.
entries.position: both — unsaved changes, The document is unsaved

entries.meaning: Unsavory has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He got mixed up with some unsavory characters downtown.
The report revealed unsavory details about the company.
The bar has an unsavory reputation.
The stew was gray and frankly unsavory.
An unsavory smell came from the refrigerator.

senses.head: Morally unpleasant; the kind of person or business you would not want to be seen with
examples: He got mixed up with some unsavory characters downtown.
The report revealed unsavory details about the company.
The bar has an unsavory reputation.

senses.head: Unpleasant to taste or smell
examples: The stew was gray and frankly unsavory.
An unsavory smell came from the refrigerator.

entries.contrast: American spelling is unsavory; British books print unsavoury. The usual meaning today is moral, not about food.

entries.meaning: Not hurt or damaged at all by something dangerous. ---
examples: Both drivers walked away unscathed.
The old church came through the fire unscathed.
Her career emerged unscathed from the scandal.
entries.position: predicative only — after escape, emerge, come through or survive
entries.contrast: It almost never stands before a noun. Say He walked away unscathed, not an unscathed man.

entries.meaning: Not planned in advance, and not on the official schedule. ---
examples: The plane made an unscheduled landing in Denver.
We had an unscheduled visit from the fire marshal.
An unscheduled power outage shut the lab for a day.

entries.meaning: Not following the methods of science; not based on evidence. ---
examples: My survey of six friends was thoroughly unscientific.
The claim rests on unscientific reasoning.
Testing one sample is an unscientific way to decide.

entries.meaning: Not written or rehearsed in advance. ---
examples: The best part of the show was an unscripted moment with the audience.
He gave an unscripted answer that made headlines.
Their conversation felt completely unscripted.

entries.meaning: Willing to cheat or hurt people to get what you want. ---
examples: Unscrupulous landlords take advantage of new arrivals.
The fund was run by an unscrupulous broker.
He is ambitious but not unscrupulous.

entries.meaning: Not closed tightly, or no longer kept closed. ---
examples: The envelope arrived unsealed.
Do not store flour in an unsealed container.
The court records were unsealed last week.

entries.meaning: Not the weather you expect at that time of year. ---
examples: We got unseasonable heat in early April.
An unseasonable frost killed the young plants.
The rain was heavy and quite unseasonable.
entries.русский: не по сезону, несвойственный времени года
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unseasonable warmth
entries.contrast: The adverb unseasonably is far more common than the adjective: unseasonably warm for October. Do not confuse it with unseasoned, which is about food without salt or spices.

entries.meaning: Unseasoned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Plain unseasoned chicken tastes like cardboard.
The rice came to the table unseasoned.
The team started an unseasoned rookie at quarterback.
An unseasoned manager might have panicked.

senses.head: Cooked without salt, pepper or other flavorings
examples: Plain unseasoned chicken tastes like cardboard.
The rice came to the table unseasoned.

senses.head: Without experience in a job, especially compared with older colleagues
examples: The team started an unseasoned rookie at quarterback.
An unseasoned manager might have panicked.

entries.position: both — the 'inexperienced' sense goes before a noun

entries.meaning: Unsecured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Credit card debt is unsecured, so the rate is higher.
The bank offers small unsecured loans to new customers.
Never log in to your bank on an unsecured network.
The ladder was left unsecured in the back of the truck.

senses.head: Of a loan or debt, not backed by property the lender can take
examples: Credit card debt is unsecured, so the rate is higher.
The bank offers small unsecured loans to new customers.

senses.head: Not locked, fastened or protected
examples: Never log in to your bank on an unsecured network.
The ladder was left unsecured in the back of the truck.

entries.meaning: Not given a ranking in a tournament draw. ---
examples: An unseeded teenager beat the defending champion.
She went into the tournament unseeded.
Two unseeded players reached the semifinals.
entries.position: both — an unseeded player, She was unseeded
entries.contrast: A sports word. In tennis the top players are ranked, or seeded, before a tournament; everyone else is unseeded.

entries.meaning: Not proper for the occasion, in a way that embarrasses people. ---
examples: There was an unseemly scramble for the last seats.
Arguing over money at a funeral is unseemly.
The senator called the remark unseemly and beneath the office.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an unseemly argument
entries.contrast: The -ly ending makes it look like an adverb, but it is an adjective. Say He behaved in an unseemly way, not He behaved unseemly.

entries.meaning: Not seen or noticed by anyone. ---
examples: She slipped out the back door unseen.
An unseen hand seems to be guiding the market.
The museum is showing previously unseen photographs.
entries.position: both — also after the noun: forces unseen
entries.contrast: Sight unseen is a fixed phrase meaning without looking at the thing first: He bought the car sight unseen.

entries.meaning: Putting other people first instead of yourself. ---
examples: It was an unselfish decision to give up the room.
The point guard is famous for unselfish passing.
She is the most unselfish person I know.

entries.meaning: Written or prepared but never sent. ---
examples: She kept a folder of unsent letters to her father.
The email sat unsent in my drafts for a week.
He found an unsent text on her phone.

entries.meaning: Looking at things plainly, without letting feelings soften the picture. ---
examples: The book gives an unsentimental account of the war.
She was unsentimental about selling the old house.
He has an unsentimental view of what the team needs.

entries.meaning: Unsettled has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The question of who pays is still unsettled.
Several claims remain unsettled after two years.
The law in this area is unsettled.
The news left me unsettled all afternoon.
The baby was unsettled after the long flight.
The forecast calls for unsettled weather through the weekend.
Conditions stayed unsettled until Thursday.

senses.head: Not decided or finished
examples: The question of who pays is still unsettled.
Several claims remain unsettled after two years.
The law in this area is unsettled.

senses.head: Uneasy and worried, unable to relax
examples: The news left me unsettled all afternoon.
The baby was unsettled after the long flight.

senses.head: Of weather, likely to change and turn bad
examples: The forecast calls for unsettled weather through the weekend.
Conditions stayed unsettled until Thursday.

entries.meaning: Unsexy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Maintenance is the unsexy part of the job that keeps everything running.
It is an unsexy topic, but it decides the budget.
Reliable and boring beats exciting and broken, however unsexy that sounds.
He complained that the uniform was deeply unsexy.
There is nothing unsexy about confidence.

senses.head: Dull, not exciting, and so easy to ignore
examples: Maintenance is the unsexy part of the job that keeps everything running.
It is an unsexy topic, but it decides the budget.
Reliable and boring beats exciting and broken, however unsexy that sounds.

senses.head: Not physically attractive
examples: He complained that the uniform was deeply unsexy.
There is nothing unsexy about confidence.

entries.meaning: Freed from something that was holding you back. ---
examples: Unshackled from the old contract, the band recorded whatever it wanted.
Critics warned about an unshackled presidency.
He played like a man unshackled.
entries.takes: from or by + noun (unshackled from the rules)

entries.meaning: So firm that nothing can change it. ---
examples: She has an unshakable belief in her students.
His confidence at the plate is unshakable.
The two men formed an unshakable friendship.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unshakable faith
entries.contrast: Also spelled unshakeable; American writing prefers unshakable. It describes beliefs and feelings, not physical objects.

entries.meaning: Still as firm as before, in spite of what happened. ---
examples: Her faith in him was unshaken.
The coach seemed unshaken by the loss.
Support for the plan remains unshaken.
entries.position: predicative only — his faith remained unshaken
entries.contrast: Unshaken says that something did not change under pressure; unshakable says that nothing ever could.

entries.meaning: Not having shaved, so the face looks rough. ---
examples: He came to the door unshaven and half asleep.
An unshaven man in a gray coat was waiting outside.
She liked him better unshaven.
entries.position: both — an unshaven face, He was unshaven
entries.form: un- + shaven, an old participle of shave

entries.meaning: Ugly to look at. ---
examples: An unsightly pile of trash had built up behind the store.
The cream is supposed to hide unsightly scars.
The new fence is frankly unsightly.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unsightly stains
entries.contrast: Another -ly adjective, never an adverb. It is about how something looks, not about eyesight.

entries.meaning: Unsigned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bank returned the unsigned check.
An unsigned note was taped to the door.
The contract is still unsigned.
The festival gives a slot to one unsigned band each year.
He was unsigned until the second week of free agency.

senses.head: Without a signature, and so not yet valid
examples: The bank returned the unsigned check.
An unsigned note was taped to the door.
The contract is still unsigned.

senses.head: Of a musician or athlete, not under contract with a label or team
examples: The festival gives a slot to one unsigned band each year.
He was unsigned until the second week of free agency.

entries.meaning: Impossible to sink, or, of a person, impossible to defeat. ---
examples: The ship was advertised as unsinkable.
This little boat is practically unsinkable.
She is the unsinkable candidate who survives every scandal.

entries.meaning: Unskilled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The factory hired mostly unskilled workers.
He arrived in the city young and unskilled.
Unskilled labor pays less than it used to.
Most of the summer jobs were unskilled.

senses.head: Of a person, having no special training for a job
examples: The factory hired mostly unskilled workers.
He arrived in the city young and unskilled.

senses.head: Of work, needing no special training
examples: Unskilled labor pays less than it used to.
Most of the summer jobs were unskilled.

entries.takes: in or at + noun (unskilled in negotiation)

entries.meaning: Not enjoying the company of other people. ---
examples: He is not rude, just unsociable after a long day.
I felt unsociable and skipped the party.
Her unsociable roommate never came out of her room.
entries.contrast: Unsociable only means not fond of company. Antisocial is much stronger and means harmful to other people: antisocial behavior.

entries.meaning: Still not bought by anyone. ---
examples: Unsold tickets go on sale at half price an hour before the show.
The house sat unsold for most of the year.
The store donates unsold bread to a shelter.

entries.meaning: Sent or given without being asked for. ---
examples: My aunt is a rich source of unsolicited advice.
The company does not accept unsolicited manuscripts.
We get a dozen unsolicited emails a day.

entries.meaning: Impossible to solve. ---
examples: The puzzle turned out to be unsolvable.
Traffic here feels like an unsolvable problem.
No problem in this class is unsolvable.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with seemingly or apparently
entries.contrast: Unsolvable means there is no possible answer; unsolved means nobody has found the answer yet.

entries.meaning: Still without an answer, and in police work still without an arrest. ---
examples: The case has been unsolved since 1978.
The city has dozens of unsolved burglaries.
One famous math problem remains unsolved.

entries.meaning: Unsophisticated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The attack used unsophisticated tools that anyone can download.
Their testing was unsophisticated but good enough.
He played an unsophisticated country lawyer.
I felt unsophisticated next to her friends from New York.

senses.head: Of equipment or methods, simple and basic
examples: The attack used unsophisticated tools that anyone can download.
Their testing was unsophisticated but good enough.

senses.head: Of a person, having little experience of art, fashion or city life
examples: He played an unsophisticated country lawyer.
I felt unsophisticated next to her friends from New York.

entries.meaning: Unsound has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The argument is unsound because it rests on one bad number.
Economists called the policy financially unsound.
The inspector found the roof structurally unsound.
They tore down the unsound porch.

senses.head: Of reasoning or a plan, not based on good judgment or good evidence
examples: The argument is unsound because it rests on one bad number.
Economists called the policy financially unsound.

senses.head: Of a building or structure, not safe or solid
examples: The inspector found the roof structurally unsound.
They tore down the unsound porch.

entries.contrast: In legal writing of unsound mind means not mentally able to make decisions. Outside that phrase, do not use unsound about people.

entries.meaning: Unsparing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The review was unsparing about the acting.
She is unsparing in her judgment of her own work.
He was unsparing with his time when a student needed help.
Their unsparing support kept the shelter open.

senses.head: Holding nothing back in criticism, and so harsh
examples: The review was unsparing about the acting.
She is unsparing in her judgment of her own work.

senses.head: Giving freely and without limit
examples: He was unsparing with his time when a student needed help.
Their unsparing support kept the shelter open.

entries.takes: in + noun or -ing (unsparing in her criticism)
entries.contrast: Two nearly opposite meanings, and only the context tells them apart: unsparing criticism is harsh, unsparing generosity is large-hearted.

entries.meaning: Too extreme to describe, almost always about something terrible. ---
examples: The children suffered unspeakable cruelty.
What happened in that village was unspeakable.
She lived through unspeakable loss and kept working.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with almost or truly

entries.meaning: Not giving details, so it could mean almost anything. ---
examples: His promises were warm but unspecific.
The complaint was so unspecific that we could not act on it.
She gave an unspecific answer about the date.
entries.contrast: In medicine the usual word is nonspecific (nonspecific symptoms), and in everyday speech Americans more often say vague.

entries.meaning: Not named or stated, usually on purpose. ---
examples: The case was settled for an unspecified sum.
He will be away for an unspecified period.
The company cited unspecified security concerns.

entries.meaning: Solid enough but not impressive or exciting. ---
examples: He had a long, unspectacular career as a backup catcher.
The results were steady and unspectacular.
It was an unspectacular meal at a fair price.

entries.meaning: Not yet used up, said of money or energy. ---
examples: Unspent funds go back to the state at the end of the year.
He came home with most of his allowance unspent.
The boy has a lot of unspent energy by bedtime.

entries.meaning: Unspoiled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They camped on an unspoiled stretch of coast.
The valley is one of the last unspoiled places in the state.
Fame has left her completely unspoiled.
The children were polite and unspoiled.

senses.head: Of a place, still beautiful because nothing has been built on it
examples: They camped on an unspoiled stretch of coast.
The valley is one of the last unspoiled places in the state.

senses.head: Of a person, not made selfish by money or success
examples: Fame has left her completely unspoiled.
The children were polite and unspoiled.

entries.contrast: American spelling is unspoiled; British books print unspoilt.

entries.meaning: Understood by everyone but never stated out loud. ---
examples: There is an unspoken rule about the parking spots.
They had an unspoken agreement never to mention it.
His disappointment stayed unspoken.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an unspoken rule
entries.contrast: An unspoken agreement is understood by everyone without being stated. Something unsaid was simply never said at all.

entries.meaning: Not fair or not respectful toward opponents. ---
examples: He was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct.
Taunting the goalie is unsportsmanlike.
The coach apologized for his unsportsmanlike remarks.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unsportsmanlike conduct
entries.contrast: Unsportsmanlike conduct is the name of the penalty in American football and basketball, so this is the form you hear on TV.

entries.meaning: Unstable has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Do not stand on that ladder, it is unstable.
The shelf is unstable without the back panel.
The region has been politically unstable for a decade.
Prices are unstable this quarter.
The note came from someone clearly unstable.
He grew more unstable in the months before the arrest.

senses.head: Not firm, and likely to fall or move
examples: Do not stand on that ladder, it is unstable.
The shelf is unstable without the back panel.

senses.head: Likely to change suddenly for the worse, said of a situation
examples: The region has been politically unstable for a decade.
Prices are unstable this quarter.

senses.head: Of a person, having sudden changes of mood or mental state
examples: The note came from someone clearly unstable.
He grew more unstable in the months before the arrest.

entries.meaning: Not said directly, though it is part of the thinking. ---
examples: The plan rests on an unstated assumption about growth.
His real reason went unstated.
There is an unstated rule that juniors answer the phone.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an unstated assumption

entries.meaning: Unsteady has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She was still unsteady on her feet after the surgery.
The table is unsteady on this floor.
He poured the coffee with an unsteady hand.
Her voice was unsteady when she read the letter.

senses.head: Not firm on its feet or its base, so it might fall
examples: She was still unsteady on her feet after the surgery.
The table is unsteady on this floor.

senses.head: Shaking, or not staying at one level
examples: He poured the coffee with an unsteady hand.
Her voice was unsteady when she read the letter.

entries.meaning: Given generously and without holding anything back. ---
examples: Her parents gave unstinting support through school.
He was unstinting in his praise of the team.
The town offered unstinting help to the families.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unstinting support
entries.form: un- + stinting, from stint (to hold back)

entries.meaning: Impossible to stop. ---
examples: In the second half she was unstoppable.
The technology now looks unstoppable.
They built a seemingly unstoppable lead.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with seemingly, virtually or truly

entries.meaning: Without a fixed plan, order or organization. ---
examples: Kids need unstructured time to play.
The interview was deliberately unstructured.
Most of the data we collect is unstructured.

entries.meaning: Not backed up by evidence. ---
examples: The paper would not print unsubstantiated claims.
Two of the three complaints were unsubstantiated.
His story remains unsubstantiated.

entries.meaning: Obvious and heavy-handed, when something gentler was called for. ---
examples: He made an unsubtle hint about the bill.
The movie has an unsubtle message about greed.
Her glance at the clock was distinctly unsubtle.
entries.contrast: The b is silent, as in subtle: uhn-SUHT-uhl.

entries.meaning: Not achieving what was wanted. ---
examples: After an unsuccessful first surgery, he tried a different hospital.
She was unsuccessful in her run for mayor.
The rescue attempt was unsuccessful.
entries.takes: in + noun or -ing (unsuccessful in finding work)

entries.meaning: Not right for a particular purpose, person or occasion. ---
examples: The film is unsuitable for young children.
She wore shoes that were unsuitable for hiking.
They called it an unsuitable site for housing.
entries.position: both — unsuitable shoes, The room is unsuitable
entries.contrast: Unsuitable goes comfortably before a noun; unsuited almost always follows a verb and takes to or for.

entries.meaning: Not having the right qualities for something or someone. ---
examples: He is unsuited to a job with that much travel.
The soil here is unsuited for corn.
They were badly unsuited to each other.
entries.position: predicative only — He is unsuited to the job
entries.takes: to or for + noun (unsuited to office work)
entries.contrast: Do not use it before a noun. Say an unsuitable candidate, but The candidate is unsuited to the job.

entries.meaning: Doing important work that nobody praises. ---
examples: School nurses are the unsung heroes of the district.
He was the unsung star of the defense.
The book is about the unsung women who ran the lab.
entries.form: un- + sung, from the old sense of songs praising someone
entries.contrast: In practice it appears almost only in unsung hero and unsung heroes.

entries.meaning: Without an adult or a manager watching. ---
examples: Never leave a toddler unsupervised near the pool.
Unsupervised screen time adds up fast.
The interns were working unsupervised all summer.
entries.position: both — unsupervised children, The kids were unsupervised

entries.meaning: Unsupported has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The claim is unsupported by any data.
The judge threw out the unsupported allegations.
That phone runs an unsupported version of the operating system.
The browser is unsupported after January.

senses.head: Not backed by evidence or facts
examples: The claim is unsupported by any data.
The judge threw out the unsupported allegations.

senses.head: No longer maintained or made to work, said of software and devices
examples: That phone runs an unsupported version of the operating system.
The browser is unsupported after January.

entries.meaning: Not giving encouragement or help to someone who needs it. ---
examples: Her family was unsupportive when she changed careers.
He works for an unsupportive manager.
I do not mean to be unsupportive, but the numbers worry me.

entries.meaning: Unsure has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I am unsure about the date of the meeting.
She was unsure whether to take the offer.
He looked unsure what to say next.
He is still unsure of himself in front of a class.
She was shy and unsure at fifteen.

senses.head: Not certain about a fact or a decision
examples: I am unsure about the date of the meeting.
She was unsure whether to take the offer.
He looked unsure what to say next.

senses.head: Lacking confidence in yourself
examples: He is still unsure of himself in front of a class.
She was shy and unsure at fifteen.

entries.position: predicative only — I am unsure; before a noun use uncertain
entries.takes: about or of + noun; a wh-clause (unsure what to do); whether-clause

entries.meaning: Better than anything else of its kind. ---
examples: The view from the ridge is unsurpassed.
She had an unsurpassed record in the 400 meters.
The shop is unsurpassed for repairs of this kind.
entries.position: both — also after the noun: a record unsurpassed for forty years
entries.takes: in or for + noun (unsurpassed in quality)

entries.meaning: Just what you would expect. ---
examples: The result was unsurprising to anyone who follows the team.
It is unsurprising that prices went up.
She gave the unsurprising answer that she needed more time.
entries.contrast: The adverb unsurprisingly is even more common and usually opens the sentence: Unsurprisingly, nobody came.

entries.meaning: Not knowing that something bad is about to happen. ---
examples: The scam targets unsuspecting older customers.
He walked into the room, entirely unsuspecting.
They sold the fake tickets to unsuspecting fans.

entries.meaning: With no sugar or sweetener added. ---
examples: I drink my iced tea unsweetened.
The recipe uses unsweetened cocoa powder.
Check the label, since most of these brands are not unsweetened.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: unsweetened tea

entries.meaning: Never turning aside from a belief, a purpose or a person. ---
examples: He showed unswerving loyalty to his old coach.
Her unswerving devotion to the work kept the project alive.
The company has an unswerving focus on safety.
entries.form: un- + swerving, from swerve (to turn aside)

entries.meaning: Unsympathetic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The doctor was competent but unsympathetic.
She gave an unsympathetic shrug and went back to work.
The court has been unsympathetic to these arguments.
Management is unsympathetic toward the union.

senses.head: Not feeling or showing pity for someone in trouble
examples: The doctor was competent but unsympathetic.
She gave an unsympathetic shrug and went back to work.

senses.head: Not in favor of an idea, a group or a plan
examples: The court has been unsympathetic to these arguments.
Management is unsympathetic toward the union.

entries.takes: to or toward + noun (unsympathetic to the strikers)
entries.contrast: A false friend: English sympathetic has nothing to do with Russian симпатичный. It means feeling for someone, so unsympathetic means cold, not ugly.

entries.meaning: Not spoiled by something bad that touched everything around it. ---
examples: He left office untainted by the scandal.
The evidence must stay untainted.
It was one of the few untainted wells in the area.

entries.meaning: Wild, not controlled by people. ---
examples: The island still has untamed forest at its center.
These horses are untamed.
He wrote about the untamed energy of the city.

entries.meaning: Available but not yet used. ---
examples: The kid has a lot of untapped potential.
Rural areas are an untapped market for the service.
The country has untapped reserves of natural gas.

entries.meaning: Untarnished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His record is untarnished after thirty years on the bench.
Her reputation came through the trial untarnished.
The silver was untarnished in its lined box.
An untarnished brass plate marked the door.

senses.head: Of a reputation, still clean and respected
examples: His record is untarnished after thirty years on the bench.
Her reputation came through the trial untarnished.

senses.head: Of metal, still bright and not dull
examples: The silver was untarnished in its lined box.
An untarnished brass plate marked the door.

entries.meaning: Not having tax charged on it. ---
examples: The first part of the benefit is untaxed.
The state is losing money to untaxed online sales.
He kept the tips untaxed and off the books.

entries.meaning: Impossible to defend or to keep going. ---
examples: His position on the board became untenable.
That argument is untenable once you read the data.
Rising rents made staying in the city untenable.
entries.comparison: more/most — more untenable, most untenable; often increasingly untenable
entries.form: un- + tenable, from Latin tenere (to hold)

entries.meaning: Untested has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The treatment is promising but untested in humans.
Thousands of kits sat untested in storage.
The team is starting an untested quarterback.
She is smart but untested in a crisis.

senses.head: Not yet tried out, so nobody knows if it works
examples: The treatment is promising but untested in humans.
Thousands of kits sat untested in storage.

senses.head: Of a person, not yet proven in a difficult situation
examples: The team is starting an untested quarterback.
She is smart but untested in a crisis.

entries.meaning: No longer tied to anything, in fact or in a figure of speech. ---
examples: An untethered balloon drifted over the field.
Stock prices seem untethered from company earnings.
After the layoff he felt completely untethered.
entries.form: un- + tethered, from tether (a rope that holds an animal)

entries.meaning: So shocking or extreme that you cannot imagine it happening. ---
examples: Twenty years ago this would have been unthinkable.
It is unthinkable that they would close the hospital.
The war forced families into unthinkable choices.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: It was unthinkable
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with almost or simply
entries.takes: that-clause (unthinkable that she would lie); to-infinitive (unthinkable to refuse)

entries.meaning: Not frightening or dangerous, and easy to be around. ---
examples: He has a quiet, unthreatening manner with patients.
The dog looked big but unthreatening.
They wanted a mascot that was friendly and unthreatening.

entries.meaning: Not neat; with things left out of place. ---
examples: His desk is permanently untidy.
She came in with untidy hair and muddy boots.
The garage got untidier every weekend.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — untidier, untidiest; more untidy, most untidy
entries.contrast: Americans usually say messy about a room and unkempt about a person; untidy sounds a little formal or British.

entries.meaning: With the knot loose or undone. ---
examples: Your shoelace is untied.
He walked around all day with an untied apron.
The boat was left untied at the dock.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: your shoelace is untied
entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: untied (not tied) is one letter away from united.

entries.meaning: Untimely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The article marked the tenth year since his untimely death.
An untimely frost ruined the crop.
Her joke was untimely, to say the least.
The report landed at an untimely point in the campaign.

senses.head: Happening far too early, especially of a death
examples: The article marked the tenth year since his untimely death.
An untimely frost ruined the crop.

senses.head: Coming at a bad moment
examples: Her joke was untimely, to say the least.
The report landed at an untimely point in the campaign.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: his untimely death
entries.contrast: It ends in -ly but it is an adjective, not an adverb. Say The remark came at an untimely moment, not He spoke untimely.

entries.meaning: Working on and on without getting tired or giving up. ---
examples: We thanked the volunteers for their untiring work.
She was untiring in her support of the library.
He is an untiring advocate for these families.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: untiring efforts

entries.meaning: Having no title or name. ---
examples: The gallery is showing an untitled painting from 1962.
He is working on an as yet untitled album.
The album is still untitled.

entries.meaning: Untold has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The storm did untold damage to the coast.
The family had untold wealth.
The film covers the untold story of the first crew.
Her side of it remains the untold part.

senses.head: Too great to be counted or measured
examples: The storm did untold damage to the coast.
The family had untold wealth.

senses.head: Never told to anyone
examples: The film covers the untold story of the first crew.
Her side of it remains the untold part.

entries.position: attributive only — untold damage, the untold story

entries.meaning: Untouchable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: For years the coach was untouchable at that school.
The program is politically untouchable.
Nobody in this company is untouchable.
On clay she was simply untouchable.
They built an untouchable lead by halftime.

senses.head: Safe from punishment, criticism or being fired
examples: For years the coach was untouchable at that school.
The program is politically untouchable.
Nobody in this company is untouchable.

senses.head: So good that no one can match it
examples: On clay she was simply untouchable.
They built an untouchable lead by halftime.

entries.meaning: Untouched has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She left her dinner untouched.
The money sat untouched in the account for years.
She sent back an untouched plate of pasta.
Two blocks were untouched by the fire.
No family in the town was left untouched by the closing.

senses.head: Not handled, eaten or used
examples: She left her dinner untouched.
The money sat untouched in the account for years.
She sent back an untouched plate of pasta.

senses.head: Not affected by something that changed everything around it
examples: Two blocks were untouched by the fire.
No family in the town was left untouched by the closing.

entries.meaning: Unexpected and unwelcome, though usually not serious. ---
examples: The nurse reported nothing untoward overnight.
The drug caused no untoward effects.
Neighbors noticed nothing untoward about the house.
entries.position: attributive only — also after nothing, anything or something: nothing untoward
entries.contrast: Formal and slightly old-fashioned. Americans say it in two syllables, uhn-TORD, and most often in the phrase nothing untoward.

entries.meaning: Impossible to follow back to its source or owner. ---
examples: The payment was made in untraceable cash.
He called from an untraceable number.
The poison is virtually untraceable.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with virtually or effectively

entries.meaning: Not taught the skills a job or task needs. ---
examples: Untrained staff were left to run the shift.
To the untrained eye the two paintings look identical.
The dog is friendly but completely untrained.
entries.contrast: To the untrained eye is a fixed phrase meaning to someone without expert knowledge.

entries.meaning: Impossible to put into another language without losing the meaning. ---
examples: The pun is untranslatable.
She says the word is untranslatable into English.
Some jokes are nearly untranslatable.
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with nearly or essentially

entries.meaning: Untreated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Untreated high blood pressure damages the heart.
The infection went untreated for weeks.
Untreated sewage was running into the river.
The deck is built from untreated pine.

senses.head: Not given medical care
examples: Untreated high blood pressure damages the heart.
The infection went untreated for weeks.

senses.head: Not put through a chemical or industrial process
examples: Untreated sewage was running into the river.
The deck is built from untreated pine.

entries.meaning: Calm, and not worried by anything. ---
examples: He seemed untroubled by the criticism.
She had an untroubled childhood on the coast.
The lake was flat and untroubled at dawn.

entries.meaning: Untrue has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The rumor is completely untrue.
The form warns against making untrue statements.
It is simply untrue that we were warned.
He had been untrue to her for years.
She refused to be untrue to her own principles.

senses.head: Not true; not matching the facts
examples: The rumor is completely untrue.
The form warns against making untrue statements.
It is simply untrue that we were warned.

senses.head: Not faithful or loyal to someone
examples: He had been untrue to her for years.
She refused to be untrue to her own principles.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: That is untrue
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, simply or patently
entries.takes: to + person for the second sense (untrue to his wife)
entries.contrast: Before a noun Americans usually say false or a false claim rather than an untrue claim.

entries.meaning: Not to be trusted, whether a person or a source of information. ---
examples: Voters found both candidates untrustworthy.
The site is an untrustworthy source for medical advice.
He proved untrustworthy with money.

entries.meaning: Not telling the truth, or not true. ---
examples: He was untruthful about where he had been.
The application contained untruthful statements.
I do not think she is being untruthful, just careless.
entries.contrast: A softer, more formal way of saying that someone lied: He was untruthful about his hours.

entries.meaning: Of a shirt: hanging loose instead of being tucked into pants or a skirt. ---
examples: He showed up in jeans and an untucked shirt.
Your shirt is untucked in the back.
The dress code says no untucked shirts.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: His shirt was untucked

entries.meaning: Not able to be used, because it is broken, damaged or badly made. ---
examples: The flood left the whole first floor unusable.
Without a charger the laptop is unusable.
Half the seats have such a bad view that they're basically unusable.

entries.meaning: Unused has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has three weeks of unused vacation.
The back bedroom sits unused most of the year.
Return any unused portion for a refund.
Unused to the cold, he wore two jackets.
She was unused to being interrupted.

senses.head: Not used; still new, or never taken advantage of
examples: She has three weeks of unused vacation.
The back bedroom sits unused most of the year.
Return any unused portion for a refund.

senses.head: unused to: not accustomed to something
examples: Unused to the cold, he wore two jackets.
She was unused to being interrupted.

entries.position: both — unused to only after a verb
entries.takes: to + noun or -ing in the sense 'not accustomed' (unused to the heat, unused to being alone)
entries.contrast: Two words share one spelling. Unused 'not used' ends in a z sound, uhn-YOOZD; unused to 'not accustomed to' ends in an s sound, uhn-YOOST, like used to. After unused to comes a noun or -ing, never a bare verb: unused to working nights.

entries.meaning: Not normal or common; different from what you expect. ---
examples: It's unusual for him to call this late.
She has an unusual name.
There was nothing unusual about the car.
entries.takes: for + noun with a to-infinitive (It's unusual for her to be late)

entries.meaning: Not having been given a vaccine against a disease. ---
examples: Unvaccinated children can't enroll until the fall.
He's still unvaccinated against the flu.
The clinic tracks how many patients remain unvaccinated.
entries.contrast: With the and no noun it becomes a group noun: the unvaccinated.

entries.meaning: Unvarnished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gave us the unvarnished truth.
I want your unvarnished opinion, not the polite version.
The shelves are unvarnished pine.
We left the floor unvarnished on purpose.

senses.head: Plain and honest, with nothing softened or left out
examples: He gave us the unvarnished truth.
I want your unvarnished opinion, not the polite version.

senses.head: Not covered with varnish
examples: The shelves are unvarnished pine.
We left the floor unvarnished on purpose.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun in the 'plain' sense

entries.meaning: Impossible to check or prove true. ---
examples: The whole story rests on unverifiable claims.
Most of what he posted online is unverifiable.
Anonymous tips are often unverifiable.

entries.meaning: Not yet checked or confirmed. ---
examples: Unverified reports say the plant is closing.
The number is still unverified.
Please don't pass along unverified information.
entries.contrast: Unverified means nobody has checked it yet; unverifiable means it cannot be checked at all.

entries.meaning: Not wanted or welcome. ---
examples: The drug has some unwanted side effects.
She was getting a lot of unwanted attention at work.
Drop off any unwanted clothes by Friday.

entries.meaning: Not justified by the facts or by the situation. ---
examples: The criticism was completely unwarranted.
He called the search an unwarranted invasion of privacy.
Their fear turned out to be unwarranted.

entries.meaning: Not watching out for danger or for a trick. ---
examples: The scam targets unwary shoppers.
Unwary hikers sometimes walk right past the trailhead.
Small print like that is written for the unwary customer.
entries.contrast: Mostly written, in phrases like the unwary buyer or a trap for the unwary. In speech Americans say careless or not paying attention.

entries.meaning: Not washed; still dirty. ---
examples: Don't eat unwashed berries.
A pile of unwashed dishes filled the sink.
His hair was unwashed and sticking up in back.
entries.contrast: The great unwashed is an old, snobbish way of saying 'ordinary people' — there the word is a noun, not the adjective.

entries.meaning: Staying firm and steady; never weakening or changing. ---
examples: She has had his unwavering support from day one.
He kept an unwavering focus on the goal.
Her loyalty to the team was unwavering.

entries.meaning: Not married. ---
examples: The article was about unwed mothers in the 1950s.
The form asks whether the parents were unwed at the time of the birth.
Unwed couples weren't eligible for the benefit back then.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an unwed mother
entries.contrast: Formal and somewhat dated, mostly in unwed mother and in legal writing. Everyday American English says single or unmarried.

entries.meaning: Not wanted; causing unhappiness or discomfort. ---
examples: The bill came as an unwelcome surprise.
They made her feel unwelcome at the meeting.
It was unwelcome news for investors.

entries.meaning: Slightly ill; not feeling healthy. ---
examples: She went home early because she felt unwell.
He's been unwell for several weeks.
If you are unwell, please stay home.
entries.position: predicative only — She felt unwell; before a noun use sick
entries.contrast: Formal and softer than sick. Americans normally say I'm sick or I don't feel good; unwell belongs to notes, news and polite speech. It never goes before a noun: a sick child, not an unwell child.

entries.meaning: Bad for your health, your mind or your character. ---
examples: The diet was cheap but unwholesome.
They worried about the unwholesome influence of his new friends.
There was something unwholesome about the whole arrangement.

entries.meaning: Unwieldy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The mattress was unwieldy on the stairs.
He wrestled the unwieldy box into the trunk.
The committee has grown unwieldy — twenty-two members now.
The tax rules are so unwieldy that nobody reads them.

senses.head: Big or awkward, and therefore hard to carry, move or handle
examples: The mattress was unwieldy on the stairs.
He wrestled the unwieldy box into the trunk.

senses.head: Too large or too complicated to work well
examples: The committee has grown unwieldy — twenty-two members now.
The tax rules are so unwieldy that nobody reads them.

entries.form: un- + wieldy, from the old verb wield

entries.meaning: Not sensible; likely to lead to trouble. ---
examples: It would be unwise to sign anything today.
Borrowing that much was an unwise move.
He made a few unwise decisions early in his career.
entries.takes: to-infinitive (It would be unwise to wait)

entries.meaning: Not knowing what is really going on; doing something without meaning to. ---
examples: He became an unwitting accomplice in the scheme.
The unwitting customers paid the fee twice.
She was an unwitting participant in the study.
entries.form: un- + witting, from the old verb wit 'know'
entries.contrast: The adverb unwittingly is far more common: He unwittingly helped them. The adjective says the person had no idea what they were part of, not that they were careless.

entries.meaning: Impossible to carry out or to make work in practice. ---
examples: The plan turned out to be unworkable.
They rejected it as an unworkable compromise.
Without more staff, the schedule is unworkable.

entries.meaning: Not experienced in practical life; not interested in money or status. ---
examples: He was a gentle, unworldly man who never locked his door.
She seemed unworldly for someone who had traveled so much.
They lead a quiet, unworldly life on the farm.

entries.meaning: Not deserving something; not good enough for it. ---
examples: He felt unworthy of such praise.
That kind of behavior is unworthy of a judge.
She dismissed the rumor as unworthy of comment.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb with of

entries.meaning: Unwritten has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's an unwritten rule about taking the last slice.
The agreement was unwritten, but everyone honored it.
Unwritten office etiquette takes a while to learn.
The last chapter of the story is still unwritten.
Their future is unwritten.

senses.head: Not written down, but understood and followed anyway
examples: There's an unwritten rule about taking the last slice.
The agreement was unwritten, but everyone honored it.
Unwritten office etiquette takes a while to learn.

senses.head: Not yet written
examples: The last chapter of the story is still unwritten.
Their future is unwritten.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an unwritten rule

entries.meaning: Unyielding has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The landlord was unyielding about the rent.
Their position on the deadline has been unyielding.
The mattress was thin and unyielding.
Concrete floors are unyielding on your knees.

senses.head: Refusing to change your mind or give in
examples: The landlord was unyielding about the rent.
Their position on the deadline has been unyielding.

senses.head: Hard and not bending under weight or pressure
examples: The mattress was thin and unyielding.
Concrete floors are unyielding on your knees.

entries.meaning: Up has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Sales are up eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are up again.
Attendance was up from last year.
I was up at five this morning.
Are the kids up yet?
The server is back up.
The site should be up again by noon.
Time's up!
Your thirty days are up on Friday.

senses.head: Higher than before in amount, level or price
examples: Sales are up eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are up again.
Attendance was up from last year.

senses.head: Awake and out of bed
examples: I was up at five this morning.
Are the kids up yet?

senses.head: Working; running normally
examples: The server is back up.
The site should be up again by noon.

senses.head: Finished, of a period of time
examples: Time's up!
Your thirty days are up on Friday.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb (Sales are up); before a noun only in fixed uses: the up escalator, an up year
entries.contrast: Up is usually an adverb or a preposition (stand up, up the stairs). It counts as an adjective when it follows be, get or seem: The market is up, Are you up? Before a noun it is rare and fixed.

entries.meaning: Not decided or settled yet. ---
examples: Our vacation plans are still up in the air.
Whether they'll move is up in the air.
The whole schedule was left up in the air after the storm.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, remain or leave
entries.contrast: Only the idiom is an adjective; The kite is up in the air is literal. It means 'not decided yet', not 'in doubt about quality'.

entries.meaning: Up to has 3 distinct senses.
examples: It's up to you where we eat.
Whether we go is up to the weather.
It's up to the manager to approve the refund.
What are those two up to?
He's up to something — he's been way too quiet.
I don't feel up to going out tonight.
He just isn't up to the job.

senses.head: up to someone: that person's decision or responsibility
examples: It's up to you where we eat.
Whether we go is up to the weather.
It's up to the manager to approve the refund.

senses.head: Doing something secret, usually something you shouldn't
examples: What are those two up to?
He's up to something — he's been way too quiet.

senses.head: Well enough or good enough for something
examples: I don't feel up to going out tonight.
He just isn't up to the job.

entries.position: predicative only — always after be or feel
entries.takes: a noun or pronoun (up to you, up to the job); -ing (up to driving)
entries.contrast: Up to is also a quantity word meaning 'as many as' (up to fifty people) and part of verbs like keep up to date. As an adjective it follows be: It's up to you, He's up to something, I'm not up to it today.

entries.meaning: Becoming successful or popular, and likely to do even better soon. ---
examples: She's an up-and-coming chef with two restaurants already.
The neighborhood is full of up-and-coming little places.
The label signs up-and-coming bands.
entries.form: compound — always hyphenated before a noun

entries.meaning: Including the very latest information. ---
examples: The app gives you up-to-the-minute traffic.
We need up-to-the-minute numbers before the call.
Their storm coverage is up-to-the-minute.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun, often open after a verb
entries.form: compound — preposition phrase used as one adjective
entries.contrast: Up-to-date is the broader word (not out of date); up-to-the-minute stresses that nothing newer exists.

entries.meaning: Cheerful and positive in mood or tone. ---
examples: The song has an upbeat tempo.
She stayed upbeat through the whole ordeal.
The report ends on an upbeat note.
entries.contrast: The noun upbeat is a musical term; the adjective is about mood. Upbeat is about how something sounds or feels; optimistic is about expecting good results.

entries.meaning: Happening soon. ---
examples: Tickets for the upcoming season go on sale Monday.
We spent the meeting on the upcoming election.
Watch your email for our upcoming events.
entries.position: attributive only — the upcoming election; after a verb say coming up

entries.meaning: Turned over so that the wrong end or side is up. ---
examples: An upended canoe lay on the bank.
The chairs sat upended on the tables.
We found the trash cans upended after the storm.

entries.meaning: Upfront has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's a $200 upfront fee.
The upfront cost is high, but you save later.
She was upfront about the risks.
I'll be upfront with you: this is going to take months.

senses.head: Paid or given before anything else happens
examples: There's a $200 upfront fee.
The upfront cost is high, but you save later.

senses.head: Honest and direct about what you think or about the facts
examples: She was upfront about the risks.
I'll be upfront with you: this is going to take months.

entries.takes: about + noun or -ing in the 'honest' sense (upfront about the cost)
entries.contrast: Also written up-front. The money sense is often an adverb, two words: You pay $500 up front.

entries.meaning: Uphill has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The last mile is a steep uphill climb.
We took the uphill route on purpose.
They face an uphill battle in court.
Getting funding has been an uphill fight from the start.

senses.head: Going up a slope
examples: The last mile is a steep uphill climb.
We took the uphill route on purpose.

senses.head: Difficult and needing long, hard effort
examples: They face an uphill battle in court.
Getting funding has been an uphill fight from the start.

entries.русский: идущий в гору; тяжёлый, требующий больших усилий
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb uphill is an adverb: The road runs uphill

entries.meaning: Belonging to the richest and highest social class. ---
examples: He grew up in an upper-class suburb.
The novel makes fun of upper-class manners.
Her background is solidly upper-class.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: an upper-class family
entries.contrast: The noun is two words with no hyphen: the upper class. In American English the label is about money and family, not about accent.

entries.meaning: Upper-level has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You need two upper-level electives to graduate.
Upper-level classes are much smaller.
The memo went to upper-level management.
Upper-level officials refused to comment.

senses.head: More advanced, of college courses
examples: You need two upper-level electives to graduate.
Upper-level classes are much smaller.

senses.head: Senior; near the top of an organization
examples: The memo went to upper-level management.
Upper-level officials refused to comment.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the wealthier part of the middle class. ---
examples: They live in a quiet upper-middle-class neighborhood.
The show is about upper-middle-class parents in the suburbs.
By any measure the family was upper-middle-class.
entries.form: compound — three words joined by hyphens

entries.meaning: Written as a capital letter. ---
examples: Type your last name in uppercase letters.
The first character has to be uppercase.
The sign was printed in uppercase type.
entries.contrast: Everyday speech says capital letters; uppercase belongs to typing, printing and password rules. Also written upper-case.

entries.meaning: Uppermost has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A few leaves still clung to the uppermost branches.
Keep the heavy pans out of the uppermost cabinet.
Safety was uppermost in her mind.
One question was uppermost: who paid for all this?

senses.head: Highest in position
examples: A few leaves still clung to the uppermost branches.
Keep the heavy pans out of the uppermost cabinet.

senses.head: Most important in someone's thoughts
examples: Safety was uppermost in her mind.
One question was uppermost: who paid for all this?

entries.position: both — the 'in someone's mind' sense only after a verb

entries.meaning: Acting as if you are more important than others think you are. ---
examples: He got uppity with the manager and was asked to leave.
They called her uppity for speaking her mind.
There's an uppity tone to the whole letter.
entries.contrast: Informal and disapproving: it says someone is acting above the place others assign them. In the United States it carries an ugly history of being used about Black people who refused to defer, so it is a word to recognize rather than to use.

entries.meaning: Upright has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Please put your seat back in the upright position.
Keep the box upright so nothing spills.
He had a reputation as an upright citizen.
She's the most upright person I know.

senses.head: Standing straight up; vertical
examples: Please put your seat back in the upright position.
Keep the box upright so nothing spills.

senses.head: Honest and behaving by the rules
examples: He had a reputation as an upright citizen.
She's the most upright person I know.

entries.contrast: Upright is also an adverb (sit upright) and a noun (an upright, meaning a piano or a post).

entries.meaning: Uproarious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The second act is uproarious.
He told an uproarious story about his first day on the job.
The joke was met with uproarious laughter.
The party got uproarious around midnight.

senses.head: Extremely funny
examples: The second act is uproarious.
He told an uproarious story about his first day on the job.

senses.head: Very noisy and full of loud laughter
examples: The joke was met with uproarious laughter.
The party got uproarious around midnight.

entries.meaning: Expensive and aimed at people with money. ---
examples: They opened an upscale steakhouse downtown.
The neighborhood has gotten much more upscale.
It's an upscale hotel, with prices to match.
entries.contrast: An American word; British English says upmarket.

entries.meaning: Making someone feel unhappy, worried or angry. ---
examples: The video is upsetting to watch.
It was an upsetting thing to hear from your own doctor.
The most upsetting part was that nobody called us.
entries.contrast: Upsetting news makes you feel bad; an upset person already feels bad: The letter was upsetting / She was upset.

entries.meaning: With the top part at the bottom. ---
examples: The map was upside-down.
She made an upside-down pineapple cake.
One of the photos got scanned upside-down.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (an upside-down cake), usually two words after a verb (The picture is upside down)
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: You're holding it upside down. The idiom turn something upside down means to search it or disturb it completely.

entries.meaning: Located on an upper floor. ---
examples: The upstairs bathroom is being redone.
We rented out the upstairs apartment.
Their upstairs neighbors play music all night.
entries.contrast: Most of the time upstairs is an adverb (go upstairs) or a noun (the whole upstairs). Only before a noun is it an adjective.

entries.meaning: Honest and respectable. ---
examples: He's an upstanding member of the community.
The defense called her hardworking and upstanding.
They seemed like upstanding people.
entries.contrast: Almost always in an upstanding citizen or an upstanding member of the community; it can sound formal or lightly ironic.

entries.meaning: New and ambitious, and challenging those already established. ---
examples: An upstart airline is undercutting the majors.
The upstart candidate finished a close second.
Upstart studios are taking market share from the big ones.
entries.contrast: Mostly a noun: He's an upstart (выскочка). Before another noun it means 'new and pushing in where nobody expected it', usually with a hint of disapproval.

entries.meaning: Upstream has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Upstream towns get their water first.
The upstream side of the dam has silted up.
The company sold off its upstream oil operations.
An upstream supplier missed a deadline and the whole line stopped.

senses.head: Closer to the source of a river
examples: Upstream towns get their water first.
The upstream side of the dam has silted up.

senses.head: At an early stage of a process or a supply chain
examples: The company sold off its upstream oil operations.
An upstream supplier missed a deadline and the whole line stopped.

entries.русский: расположенный выше по течению; начальный (в производственной цепочке)
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is an adverb: The dam is two miles upstream

entries.meaning: Nervous and tense, often about small things, and unable to relax. ---
examples: He gets uptight about being on time.
Don't be so uptight — it's just a game.
She's the most uptight person in the office.
entries.contrast: Informal. It mixes anxiety with being too strict or easily shocked, so Don't be so uptight means 'relax, stop making rules'.

entries.meaning: In or belonging to the uptown part of a city. ---
examples: They have an uptown apartment near the park.
The uptown train is running late.
It was an uptown crowd in expensive coats.
entries.contrast: American usage: in New York uptown is the northern part of Manhattan; in many other cities it is the residential part away from the business district. It is also an adverb (We're heading uptown) and a noun.

entries.meaning: Upturned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has a small upturned nose.
A row of upturned faces watched the balloon.
He sat on an upturned bucket.
Upturned boats lined the beach.

senses.head: Turned or pointing upward
examples: She has a small upturned nose.
A row of upturned faces watched the balloon.

senses.head: Turned upside down
examples: He sat on an upturned bucket.
Upturned boats lined the beach.

entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun

entries.meaning: Moving or pointing toward a higher level. ---
examples: Home prices are on an upward trend.
There's upward pressure on wages.
The chart shows a steady upward climb since March.
entries.contrast: The adjective is always upward; the adverb can be upward or upwards (prices moved upward, upwards). Never write an upwards trend.

entries.meaning: On the side that the wind is coming from. ---
examples: Take the upwind side of the fire.
The upwind boats had the advantage.
Smoke never reaches the upwind end of the camp.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is an adverb: Stay upwind

entries.meaning: Relating to a city or to city life. ---
examples: Urban schools face different problems than rural ones.
The county gets more urban every year.
She studies urban planning.
entries.contrast: Urban means 'of the city'; urbane means 'polished and sophisticated'. Different words, different stress: UR-buhn and ur-BAYN.

entries.meaning: Polite, confident and at ease socially, in a way that suggests wide experience. ---
examples: He was an urbane host who put everyone at ease.
Her writing is witty and urbane.
The ambassador is charming and urbane.
entries.contrast: Not a synonym of urban: an urbane host is smooth and well-mannered, not 'from the city'.

entries.meaning: Urgent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I got an urgent message from the school.
This is more urgent than the budget report.
Nothing on the list is urgent.
There was an urgent note in her voice.
He made an urgent appeal for volunteers.

senses.head: Needing to be dealt with right away
examples: I got an urgent message from the school.
This is more urgent than the budget report.
Nothing on the list is urgent.

senses.head: Showing that you want something done at once
examples: There was an urgent note in her voice.
He made an urgent appeal for volunteers.

entries.takes: that-clause with the base verb (It's urgent that she call us)
entries.contrast: Russian срочный can also mean 'fast': an order that has to be filled quickly is a rush order or express delivery, not an urgent delivery.

entries.meaning: Relating to urine and the organs that make and carry it. ---
examples: She's being treated for a urinary tract infection.
The urinary system includes the kidneys and the bladder.
Urinary problems are common after this surgery.

entries.meaning: From Uruguay, or relating to Uruguay. ---
examples: We went to a Uruguayan steakhouse.
The Uruguayan team won on penalties.
Her grandparents are Uruguayan.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. The same word is a noun for a person (two Uruguayans); the country is Uruguay.

entries.meaning: Usable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only half the field is usable after the rain.
Is any of this lumber still usable?
The new site is far more usable on a phone.
They redesigned the app to make it usable for beginners.

senses.head: In good enough condition to be used
examples: Only half the field is usable after the rain.
Is any of this lumber still usable?

senses.head: Easy to use, of software, tools and designs
examples: The new site is far more usable on a phone.
They redesigned the app to make it usable for beginners.

entries.contrast: The American spelling is usable; useable is a rarer variant. Note the z sound, YOO-zuh-buhl, though the noun use ends in an s sound.

entries.meaning: Familiar with something because you have done it or had it often. ---
examples: I'm used to the noise now.
It takes about a week to get used to the altitude.
She isn't used to driving in snow.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, get or become
entries.takes: to + noun, pronoun or -ing (used to the noise, used to getting up early)
entries.contrast: Two different things share this spelling. Be or get used to + noun or -ing means 'be accustomed to' (привык): I'm used to working nights.
